# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools; census records from 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 are the primary quantitative source
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron forging, paper manufacturing, early textile mills; the Housatonic and Hoosic river valleys shaped settlement patterns
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American with some Dutch families near the New York border
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker meetings in some towns; Catholic congregations begin appearing in the 1840s
- **Key historical events:** War of 1812 affected local men; canal and early railroad construction in the 1840s drew workers and shifted town populations

## Boundary changes

- Berkshire County was formed in 1761 from Hampshire County; all records predating 1761 are held under Hampshire County (Northampton)
- County boundaries were stable throughout the 1820–1850 period
- The county borders New York State to the west and Vermont to the north; families living near those lines routinely generated records in more than one jurisdiction (see Research tips below)

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** At the **town level**, Massachusetts law required recording of births, marriages, and deaths as early as 1639, though compliance varied. At the **state level**, Massachusetts was the first state to establish statewide registration, beginning in **1841** — so for your 1820–1850 window, the first two decades are town-only, and the last decade has both town and state registration. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** Births, marriages (and marriage intentions), and deaths, recorded by the **clerk of the individual town**, not the county. Each of Berkshire County's towns (Adams, Alford, Becket, Cheshire, Clarksburg, Dalton, Egremont, Florida, Great Barrington, Hancock, Hinsdale, Lanesborough, Lee, Lenox, Monterey, Mount Washington, New Ashford, New Marlborough, North Adams, Otis, Peru, Pittsfield, Richmond, Sandisfield, Savoy, Sheffield, Stockbridge, Tyringham, Washington, West Stockbridge, Windsor) kept its own registers
- **Marriage intentions** were recorded in the bride's home town and may also appear in the groom's home town and the couple's current residence — check all three
- **Published series:** The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series, published by the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), transcribes town vital records for many Berkshire County towns through 1850; this is often the fastest starting point for this period. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004500891, 512 images) of Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850. This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; it must be examined image by image with no search capability
- **Where held:** Original records remain with the clerk of each town. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds statewide registration copies beginning 1841. FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) covers this period
- **Gaps:** Pre-1841 state registration does not exist; all earlier records depend entirely on individual town compliance. Some small towns had inconsistent recording

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist churches are the most numerous and earliest; Methodist circuits were active from the early 1800s; Baptist churches in several towns; Episcopal and Quaker meetings in scattered locations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations/admissions; for Congregationalist churches, communion records and disciplinary proceedings sometimes identify family members
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004500892, 274 images) of Congregational Church Records for Pittsfield, 1791–1850. This volume is also **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (987,654 records total for Massachusetts). Many original registers remain with the individual congregation or were deposited with the Congregational Library & Archives (Boston)
- **Language:** English throughout this period

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 all cover Berkshire County; the 1850 census is the first to name every household member individually (earlier years list only the head of household with tick-marks by age range)
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 census includes a mortality schedule listing deaths in the prior year — this is an important source for death information at the very end of your target window
- **Access:** Federal census records for 1820–1850 are indexed and fully searchable on both FamilySearch and Ancestry; this is the highest-digitization record type for this period

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate estates), guardianships of minor children, inventories, and petitions; the Berkshire County Probate Court sat in Pittsfield
- **For someone who died testate** (leaving a will), search the probate series for the will and any subsequent administration filings; for someone who died intestate, search for administration packets, which often name heirs and relationships more explicitly than wills
- **Date range:** From county formation (1761) through the entire target period; there was no gap at formation since Hampshire County transferred prior jurisdiction
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Probate Court (Pittsfield). FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (567,890 records for Massachusetts)
- **Digitization level:** Collection is indexed at state scope; the survey tools did not return a Berkshire-specific volume count for probate — verify current coverage directly on FamilySearch

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England original-colony states did not use the rectangular survey system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Massachusetts is a state-land state — original grants came from the colony/Commonwealth, not the federal government; deeds were recorded at the **county** level from formation. The survey tools did not return the specific Massachusetts Land and Property wiki page; consult [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Land_and_Property) directly for the full grantor/grantee deed series description
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and attachments at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds (Pittsfield); these begin in 1761 and survive in a complete run according to the Massachusetts Genealogy wiki. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield; deeds from the Registry of Deeds have been microfilmed by FamilySearch

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (1812–1815, with pension claims active through the 1850s); Mexican-American War (1846–1848); also bounty-land warrant applications for earlier service
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at the National Archives (NARA); bounty land warrants; state adjutant general's records at the Massachusetts Archives. Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) holds War of 1812 pension and service records online
- **Note:** Pension application files for War of 1812 and earlier service often contain detailed family statements, sworn testimony about birth dates, marriage dates, and children — making them a vital-record substitute

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Every Berkshire County town has one or more town/village burial grounds; Pittsfield Cemetery, Stockbridge Cemetery, Sheffield burial ground, and Lee's Center Cemetery are among the oldest
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) has coverage for major Berkshire County cemeteries, with volunteer-submitted transcriptions and photographs; coverage is uneven for small rural grounds
- **Physical records:** Sexton record books, where they survive, remain with the town or the cemetery association; the town clerk sometimes kept burial records as part of the death register

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Berkshire County Eagle* (Pittsfield) and the *Pittsfield Sun* were both publishing in this period; neighboring Adams and Great Barrington also had local weeklies
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper digitization for this period is available on Newspapers.com ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)); microfilm runs are held at Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield Public Library's local history and genealogy department) and the American Antiquarian Society (Worcester)
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, obituaries, sheriff's sales, legal notices (estate settlements), and town meeting reports — all name individuals not found in formal registers

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Context for 1820–1850:** Large-scale immigration into Berkshire County was limited in this period, though the 1840s canal and railroad construction began to attract Irish workers; emigration *out* of Berkshire County to western New York, Ohio, and beyond was common and may require tracking the family in destination records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston is the primary Massachusetts port; New York (Castle Garden) is also relevant given the county's position on the New York border
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (indexed on FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312), 1,234,567 records); naturalization records (FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213), 345,678 records); pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record, including Berkshire County Court of Common Pleas
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town property and poll tax valuations, kept at the town level; Massachusetts state valuation lists (1820s–1840s)
- **Date range:** Town tax records exist for most Berkshire towns from formation onward; gaps exist for some small towns
- **Where held:** Individual town clerks; Massachusetts Archives holds state valuation lists. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds some transcribed tax lists
- **Substitute value:** Tax valuations for 1821, 1831, 1841 fill the gaps between federal censuses and name adult male heads of household (and sometimes widows with taxable property); essential when a person is absent from a census year

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Berkshire County towns kept detailed town meeting records naming residents appointed to road committees, elected to local office, and granted poor relief; these are at individual town clerk offices and may be partly transcribed in town histories
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published town histories (e.g., for Pittsfield, Stockbridge, Sheffield) often reprint early vital records and obituaries from newspapers no longer extant; these are available at Berkshire Athenaeum and NEHGS

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (collection 1678901); Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (collection 1459213); Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (collection 1784312); 2 digitized browse-only volumes specific to Berkshire County (imageGroupNumbers 004500891, 004500892) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection, 1820–1850 (indexed); federal census is the highest-access record type for this period | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 pension and service records; Mexican-American War records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions and photographs for Berkshire County grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Berkshire County papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military service and pension files; passenger lists | Free (NARA online) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes for Berkshire County in the 1820–1850 period. Both are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Additional Berkshire County material may appear within the broader Massachusetts state-level collections listed above, which are indexed at a higher level; the survey tools confirmed 5 such collections covering Massachusetts as a whole.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Berkshire County town clerk offices (each town) | Original town vital registers, marriage intentions, town meeting records, tax records | In-person or written request to each town |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Probate files from 1761 onward | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deeds from 1761 onward | In-person; microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield) | Local history, town histories, newspaper microfilm, genealogical collection | In-person; limited remote requests |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Statewide vital registration (1841+); state valuation lists; colonial records | In-person; some records online |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | "Vital Records to 1850" series; microfilm; manuscript collections | In-person; NEHGS members can search online |
| Congregational Library & Archives, Boston | Congregational church registers for many Berkshire County churches | In-person; some registers microfilmed |

## Records NOT online

- **Town vital registers for 1820–1840 (pre-statewide registration):** The two digitized FamilySearch volumes are browse-only and require image-by-image examination. Many individual town registers have not been digitized beyond the "Vital Records to 1850" published transcriptions
- **Town meeting and selectmen's records:** Held by individual town clerks; largely physical only
- **Town tax records:** Physical only at individual town offices; state valuation lists partially available through Massachusetts Archives
- **Berkshire County Court of Common Pleas records** (civil suits, naturalizations): Physical at Berkshire County courthouse and Massachusetts Archives; not fully digitized
- **Most church records** outside of Pittsfield's Congregational registers: Not digitized; held by individual churches or the Congregational Library & Archives

## Known record losses

The survey tools did not return any specific notices of destruction or loss for Berkshire County vital, probate, or land records. A negative search result is not evidence of loss — it is a coverage gap. If a specific record type appears absent, confirm with the holding repository (town clerk, Probate Court, Registry of Deeds, or Massachusetts Archives) before concluding records were lost.

## Research tips

- **Vital records are at the TOWN level, not the county.** You must know — or determine from census records — the specific Berkshire County town your family lived in before you can pull the correct vital register. A county-level search alone will miss the town series for 1820–1841, and even after 1841 the town register and the state copy may differ in detail. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **Start with the "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series.** NEHGS published transcriptions for most Berkshire County towns; this series is widely available in libraries and is indexed, making it far faster than browsing the original registers. Note that the published transcriptions may contain transcription errors — verify against originals for key dates
- **Cross the state lines deliberately.** The FamilySearch Wiki home page for Berkshire County did not load specific neighboring-county data during this survey. However, Berkshire County borders New York (Rensselaer, Columbia, and Dutchess counties to the west) and Vermont (Bennington County to the north). A family living near those lines likely registered events in more than one jurisdiction. New York used town-level vital registration (check the New York town clerk in the adjoining county); Vermont also used town-level recording. Research all three states' town records, not just Massachusetts
- **Marriage intentions are a distinct register.** Under Massachusetts law, couples filed notice of intent to marry at the town clerk's office, typically in the bride's home town. The intention entry often provides ages and sometimes parental names not found in the marriage record itself; it may be in a separate volume at the town clerk's office
- **The 1850 federal census is a turning point.** It is the first to name all household members individually and includes a mortality schedule for deaths in 1849–1850. Work from 1850 backward using the 1840, 1830, and 1820 censuses, which name only the head of household with age-range tallies for other members
- **War of 1812 pension files often substitute for missing vital records.** A widow applying for her husband's pension had to prove marriage and often submitted a sworn deposition naming her children and giving dates that the town vital register does not contain. Search NARA and Fold3 for any male household member of service age in 1812–1815

---

Berkshire County, Massachusetts holds its vital records at the individual town level rather than at the county courthouse, which is the most important thing to know before beginning research in the 1820–1850 period. Town registers exist from as early as 1639 in principle, though compliance was uneven; statewide registration began only in 1841. The two digitized volumes FamilySearch holds for Berkshire County in this period are both browse-only — no name index, no keyword search — so you will need to work through the published "Vital Records to 1850" town series or visit the town clerk in person for the fastest results. Because the county sits at a three-state corner, any family living near the New York or Vermont lines may have left records in Columbia, Rensselaer, or Bennington County as well, and those need to be searched separately.

The recommended next step is to identify the specific town your family lived in (the 1820 or 1830 federal census is the fastest way), then pull that town's entry in the published "Vital Records to 1850" series before moving to the original register or contacting the town clerk directly.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **⚠ Tool outage notice:** During this survey, several FamilySearch services were unavailable — the FamilySearch Wiki returned a generic stub for all Ireland-specific pages, place-search returned no results, and collections/volume search returned zero counts. All record-type sections below are based on standard Irish genealogical knowledge and the one wiki page that did load (`Ireland_Naming_Customs`). **Re-run this guide when tools are operational before relying on any absence stated here.**

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, barony of Cary, County Antrim
- **Nearest market town:** Ballycastle
- **Province:** Ulster; from 1 January 1801, part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
- **Poor Law Union:** Ballycastle Poor Law Union (established 1839) — records after 1838 may be organized by Union rather than civil parish
- **Religious communities:** Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian (various synods), Roman Catholic, Methodist

**Key events in the period:**
- 1798 United Irish Rebellion (affected all of Ulster)
- Act of Union, 1801
- Great Famine, 1845–1852 (caused heavy mortality and emigration throughout County Antrim)

---

## Boundary Changes

- Billy is a historic civil parish in the barony of Cary; its boundaries were stable throughout 1780–1870.
- Neighboring civil parishes in the barony of Cary include Armoy, Ramoan, and Loughguile — families near parish boundaries generated records on both sides.
- The Poor Law Union system (1838) created Ballycastle Poor Law Union, which governs much of Billy parish. Post-1838 records may use this unit rather than civil parish.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start dates:** Civil registration of non-Catholic marriages began **1845**; all births, marriages, and deaths from **1 January 1864**.
- The period 1780–1863 is **not covered by civil registration** — church registers are the only vital-record source.
- **Where held:** General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast (for records in present-day Northern Ireland). Civil records are indexed and searchable free at **IrishGenealogy.ie**.

---

### Church Records

- **Denominations present:** Church of Ireland, Presbyterian (multiple congregations), Roman Catholic, Methodist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry minutes; session records; communicant rolls.
- **Where held:**
  - **PRONI** (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), Belfast — holds the largest collection of County Antrim church registers (microfilm and digitized). Catalogue searchable free at **nidirect.gov.uk/proni**.
  - **Representative Church Body (RCB) Library**, Dublin — Church of Ireland registers for some parishes.
  - **Roman Catholic:** Diocese of Down and Connor; registers may remain with the parish or be at PRONI.
  - **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Belfast — Presbyterian registers.
- **Language:** English.

---

### Census Records

| Census | Status |
|---|---|
| 1821, 1831 | Largely destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire |
| 1841, 1851 | Survive in fragments for some counties |
| 1861, 1871 | Destroyed by government order before any fire |

**Census substitutes (critical for this period):**
- **Tithe Applotment Books** (1823–1837): names occupiers of land subject to tithes. Searchable free at the National Archives of Ireland online catalogue and IrishGenealogy.ie.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (surveyed 1847–1864, published for County Antrim c. 1861): names all occupiers above a minimum threshold. Searchable free at **IrishGenealogy.ie** and **Ask About Ireland** (askaboutireland.ie).

These two records together form the primary substitute for the destroyed census returns across 1780–1870.

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Pre-1858:** Prerogative Court of Armagh (higher-value estates) and the Consistorial Court of Connor (County Antrim). A large volume was destroyed in the 1922 fire.
- **Post-1858:** Civil District Probate Registry for Antrim/Ballymena established under the Probate Act 1857.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland (surviving will abstracts and indexes); PRONI (copies of many Ulster wills).
- County Antrim Quarter Sessions and Assizes records — held at PRONI; not typically online.

---

### Land Records

**Key principle:** Irish records use the **townland** as the smallest unit. Always identify the specific townland within Billy civil parish before searching — the same family can appear under multiple spellings of both surname and townland.

| Record | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1823–1837 | NAI online catalogue; IrishGenealogy.ie |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | 1847–1864 | IrishGenealogy.ie; Ask About Ireland |
| Estate papers (rentals, maps, leases) | Varies by estate | PRONI in person |

County Antrim was heavily landlord-held; **estate papers at PRONI** may name tenants in Billy civil parish by townland.

---

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** 1798 Rebellion; Napoleonic Wars (British Army); Irish Militia (active throughout this period).
- **Where held:** The National Archives (UK), Kew (War Office records; pre-1913 British Army service records were heavily damaged in a 1940 bombing — many may not survive). PRONI holds some Irish Militia records for Ulster.

---

### Cemetery Records

- Church of Ireland and Presbyterian congregations maintained their own burial grounds; Roman Catholic burials may be in separate grounds.
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) and **BillionGraves** provide some online gravestone coverage for Ireland.
- Vestry burial registers and gravestone transcriptions at PRONI supplement.

---

### Newspaper Records

- **Key titles covering north Antrim:** *Belfast Newsletter* (founded 1737), *Ballymena Observer*.
- **Digitized access:** British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk); Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, land-sale advertisements, emigration notices.

---

### Immigration and Emigration Records

- **Primary ports of emigration from Ulster:** Belfast and Londonderry (Derry); Liverpool as transit port.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at U.S. and Canadian ports; naturalization records in destination countries; Poor Law Union assisted-emigration records (post-1838); estate-assisted emigration records.
- **Where held:** U.S. arrivals at NARA; Canadian arrivals at Library and Archives Canada. Many indexed at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **Famine emigration (1845–1852):** Very high emigration from County Antrim; Famine-era passenger lists are an important source.

---

### Poor Law Records

- **Ballycastle Poor Law Union** (established 1839): Board of Guardian minutes, indoor/outdoor relief lists, death registers — may name Billy civil parish residents.
- **Where held:** PRONI holds many Ulster Poor Law Union records.

---

## Repository Summary

### Online

| Repository | What's there | URL | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil registration (births 1864+, marriages 1845+, deaths 1864+); Griffith's Valuation; Tithe Applotment | irishgenealogy.ie | Free |
| Ask About Ireland | Griffith's Primary Valuation | askaboutireland.ie | Free |
| PRONI Online Catalogue | Index to church registers, estate papers, Poor Law records, wills | nidirect.gov.uk/proni | Free (some records online) |
| National Archives of Ireland | Tithe Applotment; surviving census fragments | nationalarchives.ie | Free |
| FindAGrave / BillionGraves | Cemetery records | findagrave.com | Free |
| British Newspaper Archive | Ulster newspapers | britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **PRONI**, Belfast | Church registers (microfilm + digital), estate papers, Poor Law Union records, wills copies, freeholders lists, tithe/valuation records — **primary repository for this research** |
| **National Archives of Ireland**, Dublin | Surviving census fragments, tithe applotment, some probate |
| **GRONI**, Belfast | Civil registration from 1864; non-Catholic marriages from 1845 |
| **RCB Library**, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers (advance notice required) |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Belfast | Presbyterian registers |
| **National Archives (UK)**, Kew | British Army / War Office records |

---

## Known Record Losses

| Loss | Date | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Ireland fire | 30 June 1922 (Irish Civil War) | 1821, 1831, 1841 (mostly), 1851 (mostly) census returns destroyed; bulk of pre-1858 probate records destroyed |
| 1861 and 1871 census returns | Destroyed by government order | No census coverage for these years |
| British War Office records | Bombed 1940 | Many pre-1913 soldier service records destroyed |

---

## Naming Conventions

*(Confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki page `Ireland_Naming_Customs`)*

A traditional naming pattern was often observed by Irish parents until the later 19th century:

| Birth order | Named for |
|---|---|
| 1st son | Father's father |
| 2nd son | Mother's father |
| 3rd son | Father |
| 4th son | Father's eldest brother |
| 1st daughter | Mother's mother |
| 2nd daughter | Father's mother |
| 3rd daughter | Mother |

**Important:** This is a clue, not a rule. It was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

**Surname variations:** Mac/O' prefixes were frequently dropped or restored — the same family may appear as *O'Flynn*, *Flynn*, and *Flinn* across different records. Spelling was not standardized. Anglicization of Gaelic names produced many variants (e.g., Houlihan / O'Houlihan / Holland). Always search multiple spelling variants.

---

## Research Strategy for Billy Civil Parish, 1780–1870

1. **Start with Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books** — free, online, and the primary substitutes for the destroyed census returns.
2. **Identify the specific townland** — all Irish land records are townland-based. Correct the townland name before searching estate papers, church registers, or valuation records.
3. **Search PRONI for church registers** — the PRONI online catalogue lists all County Antrim church registers on microfilm. Presbyterian and Church of Ireland baptism/marriage registers are especially well preserved for this period in Ulster.
4. **Check PRONI estate papers** — for 1780–1823 (before tithe records begin), estate rental books and leases may be the only surviving records naming tenants in a specific townland.
5. **Search Ballycastle Poor Law Union records** (post-1838) at PRONI for any family members who received relief or died in the workhouse.
6. **Search civil registration from 1864** on IrishGenealogy.ie for births, marriages, and deaths at the tail end of this period.
7. **Check newspaper archives** for obituaries and marriage notices, especially the *Belfast Newsletter*.
8. **Search Ancestry.com and FamilySearch** for passenger manifests if family emigrated during or after the Famine.

- **Access:** No specific collection IDs, volume counts, or digitization levels were returned by any tool during this session. Researchers should search the PRONI online catalogue (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) directly.

### Census records

- **National census:** The `Ireland_Census` wiki page was unreachable. For Ireland, national censuses were taken in 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871 — all within the target period. However: the 1861 and 1871 census returns were destroyed by order of the Irish government; much of the 1821 and 1831 material was destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire; the 1841 and 1851 returns survive in fragments for some counties. These standard facts for Irish genealogy cannot be confirmed from any tool result returned during this session.
- **State/substitutes:** Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864) and the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) are the main census substitutes for this period in Ireland, but no tool result confirmed their availability for Billy civil parish specifically.
- **Access:** No indexed collection was returned by collections_search or volume_search during this session (both returned zero results due to place-resolution failure). The FamilySearch Catalog should be searched directly for County Antrim when the catalog_search tool is operational.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Where held:** The `Ireland_Probate_Records` wiki page was unreachable. Prerogative Court of Armagh (for higher-value estates) and the Consistorial Court of Connor (for County Antrim) held probate jurisdiction before the Probate Act 1857. After 1858, a civil District Probate Registry for Ballymena/Antrim was established. A large volume of pre-1900 Irish probate material was destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. No specific repository holdings were confirmed by any tool result.
- **Access:** The NAI (National Archives of Ireland) holds surviving will abstracts and indexes. PRONI holds copies of some Ulster wills. No digitized collections were returned by any tool during this session.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** The `Ireland_Land_and_Property` wiki page was unreachable. Ireland used a valuation and townland-based system, not rectangular survey. The townland is the smallest Irish land unit and the key locator for records.
- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837), Griffith's Primary Valuation (surveyed 1847–1864, published for County Antrim c. 1861), lease records, estate papers.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The land-granting authority cannot be confirmed from any tool result; the `Ireland_Land_and_Property` page was unreachable. Large portions of County Antrim were held by landed estates under the landlord system; estate papers (where they survive) are the primary land-transfer record class.
- **Where held:** PRONI holds major County Antrim estate papers. The Valuation Office (Dublin) and the National Archives of Ireland hold Griffith's field books. No FamilySearch collections or volumes were returned by any tool during this session.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** 1798 United Irish Rebellion; Napoleonic Wars (British Army service); no confirmed record-type specifics returned by tools for County Antrim specifically.
- **Record types:** British Army service records (pre-1913 largely destroyed in 1940s fire at the War Office), pension records, muster rolls, militia records. The Irish Militia was active during this period.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (UK) at Kew holds War Office records. PRONI holds some Irish Militia records for Ulster. No specific collections were returned by any tool during this session.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** The specific cemeteries serving Billy civil parish during 1780–1870 could not be confirmed from any tool result. Church of Ireland and Presbyterian congregations maintained their own burial grounds; Roman Catholic burials may be in separate grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) was included in the external_links_search results, but that link is a generic fallback result, not a confirmed Ireland-specific collection.
- **Physical records:** Vestry burial registers and gravestone transcriptions held at PRONI may supplement.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspaper titles or date ranges for County Antrim were returned by any tool during this session. The *Ballymena Observer* and *Belfast Newsletter* (founded 1737) covered the north Antrim area; these facts are not confirmed by any tool result returned in this session.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) and the Irish Newspaper Archives (https://www.irishnewsarchive.com) hold digitized Ulster papers, but neither URL was returned by any tool during this session.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, land-for-sale advertisements, emigration notices.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Belfast and Londonderry (Derry) were the primary ports of emigration from Ulster throughout this period. Liverpool was also used as a transit port.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrivals at U.S. and Canadian ports), naturalization records in destination countries, assisted-emigration records under the Poor Law Unions after 1838, estate-assisted emigration records.
- **Where held:** U.S. passenger arrival manifests are held at NARA; Canadian arrivals at Library and Archives Canada. No specific collections for Ulster emigration were returned by any tool during this session.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. The Famine period (1845–1852) produced very high emigration from County Antrim.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837, a valuation of land for tithe purposes, not a true tax list but names occupiers), Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864, names all occupiers of land valued above a minimum threshold).
- **Date range:** Tithe Applotment covers 1823–1837; Griffith's covers the 1840s–1860s survey period.
- **Where held:** Both are extensively digitized and indexed. The Tithe Applotment Books are searchable at the National Archives of Ireland online catalogue. Griffith's Valuation is indexed at Ask About Ireland (https://www.askaboutireland.ie) and at IrishGenealogy.ie. No FamilySearch collection IDs were returned during this session.
- **Substitute value:** These two records together form the primary substitute for the destroyed Irish census returns across the 1780–1870 window.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law records:** Ballycastle Poor Law Union (established 1839) records — Board of Guardian minutes, indoor/outdoor relief lists, death registers — may name Billy civil parish residents. PRONI holds many Ulster Poor Law Union records.
- **Estate papers:** County Antrim had major landed estates. Estate papers (rentals, correspondence, maps) may survive at PRONI and name tenants in Billy civil parish by townland.
- **Freeholders lists and poll books:** Surviving lists of county freeholders and election poll books (for years of contested elections) may name male property holders in the parish. PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland hold some of these.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | No indexed collections or digitized volumes were returned by tool during this session (zero results from collections_search and volume_search due to place-resolution failure); re-check at familysearch.org when tools are operational | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The place-resolution service was unavailable during this session, so collections_search returned 0 results and volume_search returned 0 results. These figures reflect a tool outage, not a confirmed absence of digitized material. Re-run the locality guide when the tools are operational.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast | Church registers, estate papers, Poor Law Union records, freeholders lists, tithe and valuation records, wills copies for Ulster | In-person, online catalogue at nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin | Surviving census fragments, tithe applotment, some probate records, state papers | In-person, online catalogue at nationalarchives.ie |
| General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast | Civil registration from 1864 (and non-Catholic marriages from 1845) for the area of present-day Northern Ireland | In-person, GRO search service |
| Representative Church Body (RCB) Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers | In-person, advance notice required |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast | Presbyterian registers and records | In-person |
| National Archives (UK), Kew | British Army records, War Office files | In-person, online at discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk |

## Records NOT online

The following record types are likely to be partially or entirely not available online for Billy civil parish in the 1780–1870 period, based on the general Irish record landscape — though specific digitization status could not be confirmed by any tool result during this session:

- Most pre-1864 Church of Ireland and Roman Catholic parish registers (may be on PRONI microfilm; browse-only or physical)
- Poor Law Union Board of Guardian minutes and indoor/outdoor relief lists
- County Antrim estate papers (rentals, maps, correspondence)
- County Antrim Quarter Sessions and Assizes court records
- Militia muster rolls and local militia records
- Pre-1858 probate records (many destroyed 1922; surviving copies at PRONI and NAI)

## Known record losses

No tool result confirmed specific record losses for Billy civil parish. The following are standard facts for Irish genealogy that cannot be confirmed from any tool result returned during this session:

- The Public Record Office of Ireland was destroyed on 30 June 1922 during the Irish Civil War, with the loss of the 1821, 1831, 1841 (largely), and 1851 (largely) census returns, and a substantial portion of pre-1858 probate records.
- The 1861 and 1871 census returns were destroyed by government order before any fire.
- British War Office records for pre-1913 soldiers were heavily damaged in a 1940 bombing; service records for many soldiers from County Antrim may not survive.

## Research tips

- **Naming conventions (confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs):** A traditional naming pattern was often used by Irish parents until the later 19th century. The first son was usually named for the father's father; the second son for the mother's father; the third son for the father; the fourth son for the father's eldest brother. The first daughter was usually named for the mother's mother; the second daughter for the father's mother; the third daughter for the mother. This pattern is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.
- **Surnames (confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs):** Mac/O' prefixes were frequently dropped or restored over time, so the same family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn across records. Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways in one parish. Anglicization of Gaelic names produced many variant forms (e.g., Houlihan / O'Houlihan / Holland).
- **Start with the land substitutes.** Since the 1780–1870 period mostly predates civil registration and the surviving census returns are fragmentary, the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) and Griffith's Primary Valuation (c. 1861 for County Antrim) are the foundational records for this period. Both are free and searchable online at IrishGenealogy.ie and Ask About Ireland.
- **Search by townland, not just civil parish.** Irish records — especially estate papers, tithe books, and valuation records — are organized by townland. Identify the specific townland within Billy civil parish before searching, as the same family could appear under multiple spellings of both surname and townland name.
- **PRONI is the key repository for Ulster church records.** PRONI holds the largest collection of County Antrim church registers on microfilm and as digitized images. Its online catalogue (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) is searchable without a visit.
- **FamilySearch Wiki unreachable during this survey (Ireland_Vital_Records, Ireland_Church_Records, Ireland_Land_and_Property, Ireland_Probate_Records, Ireland_Census, all four wiki_place_page sections for Ireland); these pages may exist — re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence.**

The most important practical warning is that the main Irish national archive was destroyed in 1922, wiping out most pre-1864 civil records and large portions of census returns — so church registers, the Tithe Applotment Books, and Griffith's Valuation become the primary sources for this period. # Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (place_search dateRange "+1811/")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data during this survey; population figures are unavailable from this run.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; Schuylkill County was the core of the Pennsylvania hard-coal region, driving heavy immigration and rapid growth in this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, Welsh, and German immigrant communities drawn by the coal industry, alongside longer-established Pennsylvania German ("Dutch") families.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Reformed, and Welsh Calvinistic Methodist congregations all present; denominations closely followed immigrant nationality groups.
- **Key historical events:** Coal boom and large-scale Irish/Welsh/German immigration in the 1840s-1860s; Civil War service 1861-1865; Molly Maguires labor conflict through the 1870s.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811. The place_search dateRange "+1811/" indicates no subsequent dissolution.
- The place_search_all tool returned no additional historical jurisdictions during this survey.
- For events predating 1811, records would have been created under an earlier parent jurisdiction; place_search_all returned no predecessor data, so contact the Pennsylvania State Archives for guidance on pre-1811 holdings.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey (URL returned: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records); specific statewide and county registration start dates could not be confirmed from a returned wiki page. output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Billy civil parish** lies on the north Antrim coast in the Barony of Dunluce, Province of Ulster — now Northern Ireland, United Kingdom. Bushmills is the principal town. The parish had a mixed population of Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian, and Catholic families throughout this period.

**Critical structural warning:** In 1922 the Public Record Office in Dublin burned, destroying **two-thirds of all Church of Ireland parish registers** and most pre-1851 Irish census returns. Records surviving before the fire are now held primarily at **PRONI** (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland) in Belfast, not in Dublin.

---

## Record Types Available, 1780–1870

### Civil Registration (Vital Records)
- **Protestant marriages only** from **1845**
- **All births, marriages, and deaths** from **1 January 1864**
- The years 1780–1863 are entirely **outside civil registration** — church registers are the only vital-records substitute for this 84-year span
- **Held at:** General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast; searchable online at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://irishgenealogy.ie) (free)

---

### Church Records

#### Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopalian)
- Registers in principle date from the 16th century, but **two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire**
- Whether the Billy parish register survived **cannot be confirmed without checking two authoritative sources**:
  1. **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** (PDF): https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf — lists every church, which registers exist, and whether PRONI holds them
  2. **RCB Library's Parish Registers List** (Church of Ireland archive): https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf
- **Held at (if surviving):** PRONI, Belfast (microfilm and digital); RCB Library, Dublin (finding aids, paid search)
- **Online:** FindMyPast holds the *Ffolliott Collection* — indexed Church of Ireland baptisms, marriages, and burials (subscription)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some vestry minute books

#### Roman Catholic
- Rural parishes in Ulster typically began keeping records **after Catholic Emancipation in 1828**; some earlier records exist
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages. Note: **Catholic registers frequently do not contain burial records**
- **Online (free):** National Library of Ireland at [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie)
- **Online (subscription):** Ancestry — *Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915*

#### Presbyterian
- County Antrim had a large Presbyterian population (Ulster Scots settlers from 1605 onward); average register start date is around 1830
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages. Note: **Presbyterian registers frequently do not contain burial records**
- **Online:** FindMyPast — *Ireland, Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms; Non-Conformist Marriages; Non-Conformist Burials* (subscription)
- **Held at:** PRONI (microfilm); Ulster Historical Foundation, [ancestryireland.com](http://www.ancestryireland.com/) (indexes, fee per search) — specializes in north Ulster

> **Tip:** Always search Church of Ireland records regardless of your ancestor's religion. In rural County Antrim, the CoI vestry often held the **only** burial register in the locality; Catholic and Presbyterian families appear in it.

---

### Census Records
- National Irish censuses of 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 were **largely destroyed in the 1922 fire**
- The 1861 and 1871 returns were **officially pulped** by government order
- The 1901 and 1911 censuses are the earliest surviving complete enumerations
- **No national census returns survive for County Antrim within the 1780–1870 window**

**Census substitutes:**
| Record | Date range | Access |
|--------|------------|--------|
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1823–1837 | Free at [AskAboutIreland.ie](https://askaboutireland.ie); Ancestry (subscription) |
| Griffith's Valuation | 1847–1864 | Free at [AskAboutIreland.ie](https://askaboutireland.ie); FindMyPast (subscription) |
| Hearth Money Rolls | 1660s | PRONI (partly transcribed) |

The Tithe Books and Griffith's together effectively name every adult male householder in Billy parish and, crucially, **identify the townland** — essential for narrowing church register searches.

---

### Probate and Wills
- Pre-1858 wills were probated in Church of Ireland diocesan courts; **most were destroyed in 1922**
- Post-1858: District Registry system; PRONI holds Northern Ireland testamentary papers
- **Surviving substitutes:** Betham, Thrift, and Crossle Genealogical Abstracts (abstracts of wills from before the fire) — on **FindMyPast** (subscription)
- **Online:** Ancestry — *Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591–1866*; FamilySearch — *Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866*

---

### Land Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** and **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864)** — see above
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin** — records deeds, mortgages, and leases from 1708; survived 1922; many entries indexed
- **Estate papers** — north Antrim was landlord territory; PRONI holds estate papers of major landlord families (rent books, tenant lists, correspondence) covering Billy parish
- **Griffith's Valuation field notebooks** — at the Valuation Office, Dublin (physical only); name occupiers by townland

---

### Other Important Record Types
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (ca. 1835):** Detailed parish-by-parish statistical surveys covering population, religion, occupations, housing. The Billy parish memoir is published in full by Queen's University Belfast — a unique source for household-level data in the pre-Famine period
- **Newspapers:** *Belfast Newsletter* (founded 1737) and *Coleraine Chronicle* (founded 1844) covered the north Antrim coast. PRONI and the British Library Newspaper Archive hold runs. Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices are the main genealogical value
- **School records:** National School system began 1831; registers may survive at PRONI
- **Military:** British Army service and pension records held at The National Archives, Kew; PRONI holds some County Antrim militia and yeomanry records

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|------------|---------------|--------|
| **PRONI**, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ | Church registers (microfilm/digital); estate papers; Tithe Books; Griffith's; wills; school records; militia | In-person; online Public Search Room at nidirect.gov.uk; fee-paying copy service |
| **RCB Library**, Braemor Park, Dublin 14 | Church of Ireland register collection and finding aids | In-person; paid search at store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy |
| **GRONI**, Belfast | Civil registration from 1864 | In-person; some records at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| **National Archives of Ireland**, Dublin | Tithe Books; Griffith's field notebooks; census fragments | In-person; online catalogue |
| **The National Archives**, Kew, England | British Army records; passenger lists | In-person; many on FindMyPast/Ancestry |

---

## Summary: Church of Ireland Register Availability

**Whether the Billy CoI register survived the 1922 fire is the critical open question for this locality.** To answer it:
1. Download **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** PDF (link above) and look up Billy parish
2. Check the **RCB Library's register list** PDF (link above)
3. Check PRONI's **Digitised Church Records** page: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni

If the register was destroyed, the best alternatives for Church of Ireland families are: the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation (to establish location and household), surviving Presbyterian registers at PRONI, FindMyPast's Ffolliott Collection index, and the Betham/Thrift/Crossle abstracts for probate substitutes.

---

*Note: The FamilySearch collections-search and place-lookup tools were non-functional during this session. A fresh survey when those tools are operational may identify additional digitized FamilySearch catalog holdings not listed here. The guide above draws from the Ireland Church Records article at the FamilySearch Research Wiki and established knowledge of Ulster record survivorship.*

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland (now Northern Ireland, United Kingdom)
- **Town of interest:** Bushmills, on the north Antrim coast
- **Administrative center for County Antrim:** Antrim town; Belfast is the provincial administrative center
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Province of Ulster; under the Crown throughout 1780–1870
- **Political event affecting records:** In 1922 the Irish Free State was established. County Antrim was one of the six Ulster counties that voted to remain in the United Kingdom. As a result, County Antrim records are now split between two national archives: records created before 1922 that were held in Dublin's Public Record Office were largely destroyed in the fire of that year; records held locally (in church vestries, solicitors' offices, and the Registry of Deeds in Dublin) and surviving copies are now in the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) in Belfast. This is the single most important structural fact for research in this parish. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Population:** No population figures were returned by any tool. County Antrim was a densely settled, predominantly Protestant county throughout this period. The Bushmills area is on the north coast in the Barony of Dunluce; it had mixed Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and Catholic populations. No census figures could be confirmed from tool results.
- **Economy:** Linen weaving, fishing, distilling (the Old Bushmills Distillery was established in the area); agriculture. These industries shaped the local population and can be documented in estate records, Ordnance Survey memoirs, and trade directories.
- **Religious denominations:** For County Antrim as a whole, the 1861 census showed Church of Ireland and Presbyterian denominations together comprising roughly 60 percent of the population, with Catholics at approximately 40 percent, per the Ireland Church Records wiki page.
- **Key historical event:** The 1798 United Irishmen rebellion affected Ulster; the 1845–1852 Great Famine caused death and mass emigration Ireland-wide, reducing records after mid-century. The 1922 PRO fire destroyed two-thirds of all Church of Ireland parish registers, as stated by the Ireland Church Records wiki page.

## Boundary changes

- Billy civil parish existed as a stable unit throughout 1780–1870. No boundary changes are recorded for this period in the tool results (place_search_all was non-functional).
- Before 1922 all Ireland was governed from Dublin under Westminster; records flowed to the Public Record Office in Dublin. After 1922 County Antrim records are administered by PRONI in Belfast.
- The ecclesiastical parish of Billy (Church of Ireland) and its civil parish boundaries closely overlap, but Catholic and Presbyterian congregations had their own separate geographic arrangements that do not map onto the civil parish.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration of non-Catholic (Protestant) marriages began nationally at the **national/civil registration level in 1845**. Civil registration of all births, marriages, and deaths — regardless of religion — began nationally at the **national/civil registration level on 1 January 1864**. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **What exists for 1780–1870:** Civil registration covers only the period 1864–1870 within this target window. Births, marriages, and deaths registered from 1 January 1864 forward (and Protestant marriages from 1845).
- **Where held:** The General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI) holds Northern Ireland civil registration records from 1864. Copies are also searchable at PRONI and through IrishGenealogy.ie for some series.
- **Gaps:** The years 1780–1863 are entirely outside civil registration. For this 84-year span, church registers are the primary vital-records substitute.

### Church records

This is the dominant source for the entire 1780–1863 period and a supplement thereafter.

**Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopalian)**

- Church of Ireland parish registers in principle date from 1536, but the Ireland Church Records wiki page states plainly that **two-thirds of all Church of Ireland registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin**. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- Billy civil parish is served by the Church of Ireland parish of Billy, Diocese of Connor (this diocese covers north Antrim). Whether the Billy registers survived the 1922 fire cannot be confirmed or denied from any tool result returned in this survey. The researcher must consult two authoritative sources produced by the Ireland Church Records wiki page:
  1. **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** (PDF): https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf — this guide lists specifically which churches exist in each parish, which records exist for each church, and whether PRONI holds them on microfilm or in original form.
  2. **PRONI's Digitised Church Records page**: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1 — lists what has been put online.
  3. **RCB Library's List of Parish Registers**: https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf — the Church of Ireland's own inventory of surviving registers, showing each parish and its date range.
- PRONI (Belfast) holds the majority of surviving Northern Ireland Church of Ireland records on microfilm and in original form.
- The RCB Library (Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14; library@ireland.anglican.org) holds Church of Ireland archives, particularly for the Republic of Ireland, but also has finding aids for Northern Ireland registers. They offer a paid search service.
- Online: FindMyPast holds the **Irish Parish Register Baptisms & Confirmations, Ffolliott Collection** (index, subscription required); **Irish Parish Register Marriages, Ffolliott Collection** (index); and **Irish Parish Register Burials, Ffolliott Collection** (index). These cover selected surviving Church of Ireland registers. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some vestry minute books survive at PRONI.

**Roman Catholic**

- The Ireland Church Records wiki page states: Catholic records in Ireland began "from the mid 1700s. Most rural parishes did not start keeping records until Catholic Emancipation in 1828. Many of the city registers date from the 1750s." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- For a rural parish like Billy/Bushmills, Catholic records likely begin sometime after 1828. The exact starting date for the relevant Catholic parish (which may have a different boundary from the civil or CoI parish) was not confirmed by any tool result. The researcher should check registers.nli.ie.
- **Online access:** The National Library of Ireland's Catholic registers database at https://registers.nli.ie/ provides free online access to many Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages). Ancestry holds **Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915** (index and images, subscription). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages. The Ireland Church Records page notes explicitly: "Catholic and Presbyterian church registers frequently do not contain burial registers." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records

**Presbyterian**

- The Ireland Church Records wiki page states: "In 1605 Scottish estate owners resettled mostly Presbyterian tenants from their estates to newly established estates in Northern Ireland. Numerous registers date from the 1600's, but the average starting date for these registers is 1830." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- Bushmills had at least one Presbyterian congregation. PRONI holds Presbyterian registers for County Antrim on microfilm.
- Online: FindMyPast holds **Ireland, Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms**; **Non-Conformist Burials**; **Non-Conformist Marriages**; and **Non-Conformist Congregational Records** — all indexed, subscription required. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- Note: Presbyterian registers similarly "frequently do not contain burial registers." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- The Ulster Historical Foundation (http://www.ancestryireland.com/) specializes in Ulster Presbyterian genealogy and holds indexes to many County Antrim Presbyterian registers. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records

**Language:** All denominations in County Antrim kept records in English throughout this period.

### Census records

- **National Irish censuses** were taken in 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871, and thereafter. The censuses of 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 were largely destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire. The 1861 and 1871 returns were pulped under government order. The 1901 and 1911 censuses are the earliest surviving full census enumerations. For 1780–1870 this means **no national census returns survive for County Antrim** — this is not a tool result gap but is stated as background by the Ireland Church Records wiki context regarding the 1922 destruction.
- **Substitutes for census:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837, naming tithe-paying landholders) and Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864, a property survey naming every household head) are the principal census substitutes for County Antrim in this period. Neither was returned by collections_search or volume_search (both tools were non-functional). The researcher should search for these on AskAboutIreland.ie and through PRONI.
- **1851 Census fragments:** Some County Antrim census fragments from 1821 and 1851 were copied by the Genealogical Office and survive; PRONI may hold some.

### Probate and court records

- No tool data was returned for Irish probate collections (wiki_read for Ireland_Probate_Records returned the generic page).
- Irish wills were probated in the Church of Ireland diocesan courts before 1858 and in the Principal Registry (Dublin) and district registries after 1858. The majority of pre-1858 will records were destroyed in the 1922 fire.
- Surviving substitutes include the Betham Genealogical Abstracts (abstracts of wills from before the fire), the Thrift Genealogical Abstracts, and the Crossle Genealogical Abstracts. All three are available on FindMyPast. The Ireland Church Records wiki page describes these explicitly as "useful substitute to records lost in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- FamilySearch holds **Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591–1866** — index and images via Ancestry. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- PRONI holds some original wills and testamentary papers for Northern Ireland estates.

### Land records

- No tool data was returned for Irish land collections (wiki_read for Ireland_Land_and_Property returned the generic page).
- The key land records for 1780–1870 in County Antrim are:
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists tithe-paying landholders by parish, with acreage and valuation. Billy parish will have its own volume. Searchable online at AskAboutIreland.ie and on Ancestry.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864):** Property survey naming every household head in Ireland. County Antrim was surveyed; results are online and searchable free at askaboutireland.ie and on FindMyPast.
  - **Registry of Deeds, Dublin:** Records deeds, mortgages, and leases from 1708 onward. The registry survived 1922. Many entries are indexed.
  - **Estate papers:** The north Antrim coast was landlord territory; estate papers of landlord families (e.g., the Macnaghten and Leslie estates) may be at PRONI.
- **Survey system:** Ireland used metes and bounds; there was no rectangular survey.
- These land record statements are not from a specific tool result on Ireland land records (the Ireland_Land_and_Property wiki page did not load), but are widely documented in the Ireland Church Records page's broader context. The researcher should verify at PRONI.

### Military records

- No tool data was returned for Irish military collections.
- Relevant conflicts in the target period: the 1798 Rebellion (United Irishmen); the Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815); service in the British Army throughout. No military records specific to Billy parish were returned by any tool.
- British Army service and pension records are held at The National Archives (Kew, England). Muster rolls and pension files for Irish soldiers are searchable there.
- PRONI holds some militia and yeomanry records for County Antrim.

### Cemetery records

- No tool data was returned for County Antrim cemetery collections.
- Church of Ireland churchyards in Billy parish (including Bushmills) hold headstones from the 18th and 19th centuries. Many are surveyed and transcribed; the Ulster Historical Foundation and the North of Ireland Family History Society hold transcriptions.
- The Ireland Church Records wiki page recommends searching available Church of Ireland records even if your family was not of that denomination, because the burial register of the Church of Ireland church was often the only burial register in the locality. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- FindAGrave and BillionGraves have some County Antrim cemetery records but coverage varies.

### Newspaper records

- No tool data was returned for County Antrim newspapers.
- The key north Antrim paper for this period is the **Coleraine Chronicle** (founded 1844) and the **Belfast Newsletter** (founded 1737, one of the oldest continuously published newspapers in the world). Both covered the Bushmills/Antrim coast area. PRONI and the British Library's newspaper archive hold runs of these papers.
- Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices (land auctions, ejectments) are the primary genealogical value.

### Immigration and emigration records

- County Antrim had very high emigration rates to North America, especially after 1800 and massively after the Famine (1845–1852). The Bushmills/north Antrim area was a significant emigration source for Ulster Scots families to the American colonies and later the United States and Canada.
- Passenger lists for vessels departing from ports such as Londonderry/Derry, Belfast, and Liverpool are held at NARA (U.S.) and Library and Archives Canada.
- Declarations of intention and naturalizations for emigrants who settled in the United States are held at NARA and in local federal and state courts — these records were created inland, far from any port, and often name the townland of origin in Ireland.
- No specific collections were returned by tool results (external_links_search was non-functional).

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** County Antrim rolls survive in part and name householders; held at PRONI.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** The most important tax-substitute for the target period — names tithe-paying householders by townland within each civil parish. Billy parish will have a volume. Searchable at AskAboutIreland.ie.
- These can substitute for the missing census years throughout the entire target window.

### Other record types

- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** The Irish Ordnance Survey conducted detailed parish-by-parish statistical memoirs covering population, religion, occupations, housing, and historical notes. County Antrim memoirs were published in full by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast. The memoir for Billy parish describes the parish in detail ca. 1835 and is a unique source for household-level data in the pre-Famine period.
- **Estate records:** PRONI holds extensive north Antrim estate papers. A landlord's rent books, tenant lists, and correspondence often name individual households not found elsewhere.
- **School records:** The National School system was established in Ireland in 1831. School registers from the 1830s onward may survive at PRONI or the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Griffith's Valuation notebooks:** The field notebooks behind the published valuation (1847–1864) survive at the Valuation Office in Dublin and name occupiers by townland.

- Ordnance Survey Memoirs for Billy parish — published in book form by Queen's University Belfast; not fully digitized

- Hearth Money Rolls — physical at PRONI; partly transcribed and published

## Known record losses

The Ireland Church Records wiki page states that **two-thirds of Church of Ireland parish registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin**. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records. This is a general statement covering all Church of Ireland parishes in Ireland; whether the Billy register was among those destroyed cannot be determined from the tool results returned in this session. Check the RCB Library's PDF list and PRONI's guide.

The same 1922 fire destroyed the vast majority of pre-1858 Irish wills and most pre-1851 census returns. The 1861 and 1871 censuses were officially destroyed under government order.

The Ireland Church Records page notes that the Betham, Thrift, and Crossle genealogical abstracts are "useful substitutes to records lost in the 1922 Public Record Office fire." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records

## Research tips

- **For Church of Ireland registers specifically:** Download and search PRONI's Guide to Church Records PDF (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf). This document lists each civil parish, the churches within it, which registers exist, and whether PRONI holds them. Cross-reference with the RCB Library list (https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Search all denominations regardless of presumed religion.** The Ireland Church Records wiki page advises: "Search available Church of Ireland records even if your family was not of the Church of Ireland." In rural County Antrim, the Church of Ireland vestry often held the only consistent burial register; Catholic families appear in it. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Catholic burial records are typically absent.** The Ireland Church Records page states plainly that "Catholic and Presbyterian church registers frequently do not contain burial registers." For Catholic and Presbyterian burials, look to Church of Ireland burial registers, headstone surveys, and newspaper death notices. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) and Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864) together cover most adult male householders.** They are the effective substitutes for the missing census years and are the first step for identifying a family's townland within Billy parish before searching church registers.
- **Name the townland before searching church records.** County Antrim church registers are typically indexed only to the parish level, not to individual townlands. Knowing a family's townland (from Tithe Books, Griffith's, or estate records) allows efficient narrowing.
- **Emigration records can identify townlands.** Naturalization papers and some passenger manifests filed in the United States name the parish and townland of Irish birth. Working backward from an American record is often the most reliable way to pin a family to a specific locality within County Antrim. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records (emigration section)
- **The Ulster Historical Foundation** (http://www.ancestryireland.com/) specializes in north Ulster, including County Antrim, and holds indexes to many local Presbyterian and Church of Ireland registers not fully covered by national databases. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records

---

Billy civil parish (containing Bushmills town) sits on the north Antrim coast in what is now Northern Ireland. For the years 1780 to 1870, civil registration did not exist until 1864 (or 1845 for Protestant marriages), so church registers are the overwhelmingly dominant record type. The most important warning is that two-thirds of all Church of Ireland parish registers were destroyed in a 1922 fire, and whether Billy's own register survived must be verified directly through PRONI's online church records guide and the RCB Library's register list — both accessible through the links above. The key repository for all surviving County Antrim records is PRONI in Belfast, which holds church records on microfilm, estate papers, and the main land-survey substitutes for the missing censuses. Free Catholic register images are available through the National Library of Ireland's website. Note that several of the standard place-lookup and digitized-collections tools were non-functional during this survey, so a fresh run when those tools are operational may surface additional FamilySearch catalog holdings and indexed collections not identified here.

Once the Church of Ireland register availability question is settled at PRONI, the next step is to build a research plan using the repositories and record types identified here as starting points.
