quirks: Arkansas did not exist as a legal jurisdiction before 1819 (Territory) or 1836 (State). Before 1800, the territory was part of Spanish Louisiana, administered from New Orleans. All pre-1800 records were created under French or Spanish colonial authority, not American or Arkansas-state authority.

The only significant European settlement in the Arkansas region before 1800 was Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas / Post de los Arkansas), established 1686. If an ancestor lived in the territory, Arkansas Post records are almost certainly the relevant source.

Records for the Spanish colonial period (1763-1800) are in Spanish; records from the French period (pre-1763) are in French. A researcher must read those languages or use a translator to work the originals.

The single digitized FamilySearch volume for Arkansas Post (image group 008814402, 64 images, sacramental registers 1763-1800) is browse-only and in Spanish — it has no name index and requires page-by-page reading.

Many administrative and civil records for the Arkansas Post area were generated in New Orleans (the colonial capital) and may not appear in Arkansas-focused finding aids. Search Louisiana colonial record collections in parallel.

The Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain holds a major body of Spanish colonial Louisiana records — including military reports, padrones (census lists), and land concession files — that are not fully microfilmed or digitized and require a research visit or a commissioned researcher on-site.

The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all four Arkansas-specific place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips); Arkansas-specific research strategy was drawn from wiki_search results citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records instead.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas) established 1686 by the French; territory passed to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762, effective 1769) and Treaty of Paris (1763); retroceded to France 1800; acquired by the United States under the Louisiana Purchase (1803); Arkansas Territory created 1819; Arkansas statehood 1836.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post (only European settlement of significance in the territory before 1800).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) through 1762/1763; Spanish Louisiana (Province of Louisiana under the Captaincy General of Cuba) 1763-1800; brief French interregnum 1800-1803; thereafter United States.
- **Population during period:** The European and mixed settler population at Arkansas Post was very small — estimated at a few hundred at most during the Spanish period. The surrounding region was predominantly inhabited by the Quapaw and other Native peoples.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, small-scale agriculture, military garrison.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Canadian and French Creole settlers, Spanish garrison troops and officials, Quapaw Nation, enslaved Africans, some Anglo-American traders.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only formally sanctioned church under both French and Spanish colonial rule).
- **Key historical events:** Transfer from France to Spain (1762-1769); Spanish Bourbon reforms reorganizing colonial administration; transfer back to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763, the territory was part of French Louisiana (La Louisiane), administered from New Orleans.
- From 1763 (effective full transfer by 1769), the territory became part of Spanish Louisiana under the Captaincy General of Cuba, still administered through New Orleans.
- The territory had no internal county or parish subdivisions before 1803 — all civil authority flowed through the commandant at Arkansas Post.
- After 1803, the area was successively part of the District of Louisiana, Missouri Territory (1812), and then Arkansas Territory (1819) before statehood in 1836.
- Records created before Arkansas Territory's formation in 1819 will NOT be found in Arkansas-jurisdiction finding aids; search Louisiana colonial and Missouri/Orleans Territory collections instead.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the modern sense during the Spanish colonial period. The Catholic Church was the sole registrar of vital events.
- **What exists:** Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) maintained by Catholic missionaries and priests at Arkansas Post. These registers cover both European colonists and baptized Native Americans.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch has digitized **one browse-only volume** (image group 008814402, 64 images) of Arkansas Post sacramental registers covering 1763-1800. It is in Spanish, not name-indexed, and requires page-by-page browsing.
  - The **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** holds original sacramental registers.
  - The **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) holds transcribed versions per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records.
- **Gaps:** Registers from the French period (pre-1763) are less complete; some volumes may not have survived.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** This IS the pre-registration era. The sacramental registers are the primary vital record.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only under both French and Spanish colonial rule.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including adults and children of Native Americans), marriages, burials, and occasional confirmations.
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (original registers).
  - Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions).
  - FamilySearch image group 008814402: 64-image browse-only volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763-1800 — in Spanish.
  - The broader Louisiana Catholic sacramental register collection (FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925") covers the colonial Louisiana church network that included Arkansas Post; this is indexed and has 987,654 records, though its coverage of Arkansas Post specifically is unconfirmed from tool results.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers), Spanish (post-1763 registers), with French sometimes continued under Spanish rule.

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** The Spanish administration conducted periodic census lists (padrones) of the Arkansas Post population under Spanish administration (1763-1800). These are civil/military documents, not church records. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, padrones survive at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville).
- **Federal/national census:** The earliest federal census covering what became Arkansas is 1810 (Missouri Territory) — entirely outside the pre-1800 scope.
- **FamilySearch collection 2085124** ("Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870") begins in 1819 and does not cover the Spanish colonial period.
- **Access:** Padrones are physical records at the repositories named above. No digitized, indexed version of the Arkansas Post padrones was found in tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under the Spanish colonial commandant at Arkansas Post, civil disputes, contracts, and estate matters were handled through the military commandant's office rather than a separate civil court. Records of these proceedings, where they survive, would be filed as part of the general civil and military records of the post.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville). No digitized FamilySearch collection covering Arkansas colonial probate was found.
- **Note:** Formal probate courts did not exist in the territory before 1803.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierras) were granted by the colonial commandant or governor. These predate the U.S. rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish crown grants were issued through the colonial governor in New Orleans; the local commandant at Arkansas Post held authority to grant smaller tracts.
- **Types:** Land concessions/grants, surveys (arpents), titles. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, land concession records survive at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Date range:** Spanish land grants in the Arkansas territory date from the 1760s onward.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias; some Spanish land grant claims were later confirmed by U.S. courts and appear in federal land records (General Land Office). The Bureau of Land Management's GLO Records site (glorecords.blm.gov) may include confirmed Spanish grant claims.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War-era military operations (Spain entered the war against Britain in 1779; the Arkansas Post garrison was involved in regional actions).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, troop lists, garrison reports, military correspondence — generated by the Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville) holds the primary body of Spanish colonial military records for Louisiana. The Arkansas History Commission holds some microfilm copies. No digitized FamilySearch military collection for this period and place was found in tool results.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** Burials at Arkansas Post were recorded in the sacramental registers (see Church records above) rather than separate sexton records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) lists some Arkansas Post-area graves, but coverage of 18th-century colonial burials is minimal.
- **Physical records:** The burial register is the sacramental register — see image group 008814402 at FamilySearch and the Diocese of Little Rock holdings.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas territory before 1800. The nearest colonial press was in New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for the pre-1800 Arkansas region.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the entry point for virtually all settlers arriving in Spanish Louisiana, including those who moved upriver to Arkansas Post.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, ship manifests, and immigration permits (permisos) issued under Spanish colonial law. Some settlers came overland from the French Canadian settlements.
- **Where held:** Spanish colonial immigration and settlement records are at the Archivo General de Indias. The Historic New Orleans Collection and the Louisiana State Archives hold some Louisiana colonial immigration material.
- **Content note:** Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) often recorded place of origin, which can serve as a substitute immigration record.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax records and trade duty records for Arkansas Post.
- **Date range:** Spanish period (1763-1800).
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission. No digitized FamilySearch tax collection for this period and place was found.
- **Substitute value:** The padrones (census lists) frequently recorded property and livestock, functioning as a combined census and tax substitute.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records) covering Louisiana 1699-1769 are digitized at FamilySearch in a browse-only volume (image group 004330992, 149 images, French and Spanish). These cover the colonial administration based in New Orleans that also governed the Arkansas Post area.
- **Correspondence and reports:** Spanish governors' reports, letters from the Arkansas Post commandant, and administrative correspondence often named settlers individually. These are primarily in the Archivo General de Indias.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763-1800 (64 images, browse-only, Spanish) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records, indexed) — broader Louisiana colonial church network | Free |
| FamilySearch | Image group 004330992: French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records) 1699-1769, 149 images, browse-only, French/Spanish | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 2085124: Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 — post-1800, for continuity research only | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | glorecords.blm.gov — confirmed Spanish land grant claims in federal records | Free |

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas) established 1686 by the French; territory passed to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762, effective 1769) and Treaty of Paris (1763); retroceded to France 1800; acquired by the United States under the Louisiana Purchase (1803); Arkansas Territory created 1819; Arkansas statehood 1836.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post (only European settlement of significance in the territory before 1800).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) through 1762/1763; Spanish Louisiana (Province of Louisiana under the Captaincy General of Cuba) 1763-1800; brief French interregnum 1800-1803; thereafter United States.
- **Population during period:** The European and mixed settler population at Arkansas Post was very small — estimated at a few hundred at most during the Spanish period. The surrounding region was predominantly inhabited by the Quapaw and other Native peoples.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, small-scale agriculture, military garrison.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Canadian and French Creole settlers, Spanish garrison troops and officials, Quapaw Nation, enslaved Africans, some Anglo-American traders.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only formally sanctioned church under both French and Spanish colonial rule).
- **Key historical events:** Transfer from France to Spain (1762-1769); Spanish Bourbon reforms reorganizing colonial administration; transfer back to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763, the territory was part of French Louisiana (La Louisiane), administered from New Orleans.
- From 1763 (effective full transfer by 1769), the territory became part of Spanish Louisiana under the Captaincy General of Cuba, still administered through New Orleans.
- The territory had no internal county or parish subdivisions before 1803 — all civil authority flowed through the commandant at Arkansas Post.
- After 1803, the area was successively part of the District of Louisiana, Missouri Territory (1812), and then Arkansas Territory (1819) before statehood in 1836.
- Records created before Arkansas Territory's formation in 1819 will NOT be found in Arkansas-jurisdiction finding aids; search Louisiana colonial and Missouri/Orleans Territory collections instead.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the modern sense during the Spanish colonial period. The Catholic Church was the sole registrar of vital events.
- **What exists:** Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) maintained by Catholic missionaries and priests at Arkansas Post. These registers cover both European colonists and baptized Native Americans.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch has digitized **one browse-only volume** (image group 008814402, 64 images) of Arkansas Post sacramental registers covering 1763-1800. It is in Spanish, not name-indexed, and requires page-by-page browsing.
  - The **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** holds original sacramental registers.
  - The **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) holds transcribed versions per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records.
- **Gaps:** Registers from the French period (pre-1763) are less complete; some volumes may not have survived.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** This IS the pre-registration era. The sacramental registers are the primary vital record.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only under both French and Spanish colonial rule.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including adults and children of Native Americans), marriages, burials, and occasional confirmations.
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (original registers).
  - Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions).
  - FamilySearch image group 008814402: 64-image browse-only volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763-1800 — in Spanish.
  - The broader Louisiana Catholic sacramental register collection (FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925") covers the colonial Louisiana church network that included Arkansas Post; this is indexed and has 987,654 records, though its coverage of Arkansas Post specifically is unconfirmed from tool results.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers), Spanish (post-1763 registers), with French sometimes continued under Spanish rule.

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** The Spanish administration conducted periodic census lists (padrones) of the Arkansas Post population under Spanish administration (1763-1800). These are civil/military documents, not church records. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, padrones survive at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville).
- **Federal/national census:** The earliest federal census covering what became Arkansas is 1810 (Missouri Territory) — entirely outside the pre-1800 scope.
- **FamilySearch collection 2085124** ("Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870") begins in 1819 and does not cover the Spanish colonial period.
- **Access:** Padrones are physical records at the repositories named above. No digitized, indexed version of the Arkansas Post padrones was found in tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under the Spanish colonial commandant at Arkansas Post, civil disputes, contracts, and estate matters were handled through the military commandant's office rather than a separate civil court. Records of these proceedings, where they survive, would be filed as part of the general civil and military records of the post.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville). No digitized FamilySearch collection covering Arkansas colonial probate was found.
- **Note:** Formal probate courts did not exist in the territory before 1803.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierras) were granted by the colonial commandant or governor. These predate the U.S. rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish crown grants were issued through the colonial governor in New Orleans; the local commandant at Arkansas Post held authority to grant smaller tracts.
- **Types:** Land concessions/grants, surveys (arpents), titles. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, land concession records survive at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Date range:** Spanish land grants in the Arkansas territory date from the 1760s onward.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias; some Spanish land grant claims were later confirmed by U.S. courts and appear in federal land records (General Land Office). The Bureau of Land Management's GLO Records site (glorecords.blm.gov) may include confirmed Spanish grant claims.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War-era military operations (Spain entered the war against Britain in 1779; the Arkansas Post garrison was involved in regional actions).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, troop lists, garrison reports, military correspondence — generated by the Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville) holds the primary body of Spanish colonial military records for Louisiana. The Arkansas History Commission holds some microfilm copies. No digitized FamilySearch military collection for this period and place was found in tool results.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** Burials at Arkansas Post were recorded in the sacramental registers (see Church records above) rather than separate sexton records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) lists some Arkansas Post-area graves, but coverage of 18th-century colonial burials is minimal.
- **Physical records:** The burial register is the sacramental register — see image group 008814402 at FamilySearch and the Diocese of Little Rock holdings.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas territory before 1800. The nearest colonial press was in New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for the pre-1800 Arkansas region.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the entry point for virtually all settlers arriving in Spanish Louisiana, including those who moved upriver to Arkansas Post.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, ship manifests, and immigration permits (permisos) issued under Spanish colonial law. Some settlers came overland from the French Canadian settlements.
- **Where held:** Spanish colonial immigration and settlement records are at the Archivo General de Indias. The Historic New Orleans Collection and the Louisiana State Archives hold some Louisiana colonial immigration material.
- **Content note:** Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) often recorded place of origin, which can serve as a substitute immigration record.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax records and trade duty records for Arkansas Post.
- **Date range:** Spanish period (1763-1800).
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission. No digitized FamilySearch tax collection for this period and place was found.
- **Substitute value:** The padrones (census lists) frequently recorded property and livestock, functioning as a combined census and tax substitute.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records) covering Louisiana 1699-1769 are digitized at FamilySearch in a browse-only volume (image group 004330992, 149 images, French and Spanish). These cover the colonial administration based in New Orleans that also governed the Arkansas Post area.
- **Correspondence and reports:** Spanish governors' reports, letters from the Arkansas Post commandant, and administrative correspondence often named settlers individually. These are primarily in the Archivo General de Indias.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763-1800 (64 images, browse-only, Spanish) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records, indexed) — broader Louisiana colonial church network | Free |
| FamilySearch | Image group 004330992: French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records) 1699-1769, 149 images, browse-only, French/Spanish | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 2085124: Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 — post-1800, for continuity research only | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | glorecords.blm.gov — confirmed Spanish land grant claims in federal records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal land records, territorial-era records beginning 1803 | Free/paid |

**Coverage of this survey:** The Arkansas-specific volume_search (endYear 1800) returned 1 total digitized volume (image group 008814402), which is the complete result set — no further pages. The Louisiana volume_search returned 2 additional volumes covering the broader colonial period. These are all browse-only.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records, padrones, land concessions, transcribed church registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, AR | Original sacramental registers for Arkansas Post | Contact diocese archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial Louisiana administrative, military, land, and civil records | In-person or commissioned researcher; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of some Spanish colonial Louisiana records | In-person or Microfilm Loan Program |
| Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Archives | Louisiana colonial records including some Arkansas Post-area material | In-person or online finding aids |

## Records NOT online

- Spanish colonial land concession files — physical, at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias.
- Spanish colonial military muster rolls and garrison records — physical, at Archivo General de Indias.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Period) (1787–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from it on 1 March 1803.
- **First organized county:** Washington County, organized 1788 (seat: Marietta). Hamilton County organized 1790 (seat: Cincinnati).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory of the United States (federal authority), then Ohio (state authority from 1803)
- **Population during period:** Extremely sparse non-indigenous settlement in 1790; no population data was returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, early land speculation
- **Ethnic composition:** New England migrants (Connecticut Western Reserve settlers), Virginia veterans (Military District grantees), Pennsylvania and Kentucky migrants; indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) still held much of the territory
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Congregationalist (especially Western Reserve), Baptist, Quaker; no established institutional church presence across most of the territory in 1790
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance 1787 (created the territory and its governance framework); Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794 and Treaty of Greenville 1795 (opened more of Ohio to settlement); Ohio statehood 1803

## Boundary changes
- Before 1788, present-day Ohio had no organized U.S. county structure at all. The Northwest Territory governed the entire region from its capital at Marietta.
- Washington County (1788) encompassed essentially all of present-day Ohio and beyond at its creation.
- Hamilton County was carved from Washington County in 1790, covering the southwestern corner.
- Between 1790 and 1803, additional counties were rapidly carved from Washington and Hamilton as settlement spread. Researchers must identify the exact county that held jurisdiction at the moment of an event — a different county may have held those records even for nearby locations one year apart.
- At statehood in 1803, Ohio succeeded to the Northwest Territory's record-keeping obligations. Early territorial records did not automatically transfer to county courthouses — many stayed with the territorial administration and are now at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
- **This is a temporal split with geographic complexity**: which county holds a given record from 1788-1803 depends on both the date of the event and the precise township location, since county boundaries shifted constantly. Do not assume Washington County holds all pre-1790 Ohio records — Marietta settlers are there, but the rest of the territory was unorganized.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births or deaths existed in the 1790 period. The FamilySearch Wiki's Ohio Vital Records page returned only generic content and did not supply a specific Ohio start date; do not assume a registration date from this guide. County-level marriage records begin from 1789 in Washington County (FamilySearch collection 1803785, "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013").
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1789 (indexed, with images, 1,523,678 records covering 3,047,356 persons). No civil birth or death collections overlap the 1790 target window.
- **Where held:** County courthouse for the county of jurisdiction at the time; early Washington County records at the county courthouse in Marietta and microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** Civil birth and death registration is not documented in tool results for the pre-statehood period. This is not evidence of non-registration; it is a coverage gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers (see Church records below) are the primary substitute for civil vital records in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist (circuit riders), Presbyterian, Congregationalist (Western Reserve), Baptist, Quaker meeting records; Roman Catholic missions were present but not extensively in early Ohio interior
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some congregations kept membership rolls with family data
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has indexed 678,234 records in collection 2246917 ("Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950") with images. Denominational archives: Methodist records at Ohio Wesleyan University; Presbyterian records at Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); Quaker records at Ohio Valley Yearly Meeting. Congregationalist records often deposited with the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
- **Language:** English
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (via FamilySearch collection 2246917)

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 census covers the Northwest Territory, but Ohio settlement was so sparse that records are minimal. No distinct "Ohio" schedules exist; search under Washington County, Northwest Territory. The first census in which Ohio appears as a state is 1800, filed under Ohio counties.
- **State/territorial census:** No territorial census of the Northwest Territory is known to survive for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists (see Tax records below) serve as partial substitutes.
- **Access:** 1800 federal census for Ohio is indexed online (Ancestry, FamilySearch).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court minutes
- **Date range:** Washington County court records begin 1788; Hamilton County from 1790
- **Where held:** County courthouses (probate division) for post-1788 county records. Pre-county territorial court records at the Ohio History Connection, Columbus. FamilySearch has not returned a specific probate digitization for this pre-statehood window.
- **Digitization level:** Physical/microfilm only for the 1787-1803 territorial period — no indexed probate collection for this window appeared in tool results.

### Land records
- **Survey systems:** Ohio has THREE systems depending on location: (1) the Virginia Military District (between Scioto and Little Miami rivers) — metes-and-bounds survey used for Virginia veterans' bounty warrants; (2) the Connecticut Western Reserve (northeastern Ohio) — township grid survey; (3) the remainder of Ohio — U.S. Public Land Survey System (rectangular township-and-range grid)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal (U.S. General Land Office) for most of Ohio; Virginia for Military District warrants. BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal patents. Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library (Richmond). Connecticut Western Reserve grants are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland. (Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Types:** Land patents/grants, deeds, bounty land warrants, tax records
- **Date range:** Federal patents from 1787; FamilySearch collection 1542187 ("Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840") covers 234,567 records with images.
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 browse-only volume of Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records (1788-1799, DGS 005112233, 51 images, 0% indexed, not full-text) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch collection; browse-only for the territorial volume.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (veterans were land-grant recipients in the Virginia Military District and received U.S. bounty land warrants); Northwest Indian War (1785-1795, including the Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrant files at NARA (digitized on Fold3 and Ancestry); state service records at Ohio History Connection for Northwest Indian War militia service
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized pension files

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mound Cemetery (Marietta, 1788, one of the oldest in Ohio); early frontier burial grounds often attached to churches or on family farmsteads with no formal records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage; many early graves were never formally recorded
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive from before 1800 in Ohio

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, 1793) was the first newspaper in Ohio/Northwest Territory; extremely limited survival
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds the earliest Ohio newspaper collections; check their digital resources at ohiomemory.org
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale announcements; obituaries are rarely found this early

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia, Baltimore, and New York were primary eastern entry points; settlers then moved overland or via the Ohio River
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); territorial court naturalizations at the Ohio History Connection
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) for passenger lists; FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants. For families immigrating in this period, check the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property/personal property tax lists; these are the most consistent annual record of residents in this period
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1987542 ("Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850") covers 345,890 records from 1800. A partially-indexed FamilySearch volume of Washington County tax records 1799-1803 exists (DGS 005112240, 73 images, 12% indexed, not full-text).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch (partially indexed for 1799-1803)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records in the 1790-1800 gap and for any census year with missing schedules.

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** The Northwest Territory's legislative and executive records are at NARA (Record Group 59) and the Ohio History Connection. These include territorial land surveys, petition files, and court minutes that name settlers not found in county records.
- **Land company records:** The Ohio Company of Associates (Marietta area) and the John Cleves Symmes Purchase (Miami Valley) left company records naming early purchasers. Ohio Company records are at Marietta College's archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records 1788-1799 (browse-only, 51 images); Washington County Tax Records 1799-1803 (73 images, 12% indexed) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents and surveys | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| NARA | Revolutionary War pensions, bounty land warrants, passenger lists | Free catalog; Fold3/Ancestry for digitized files |
| Fold3 | Military pension files and service records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (partial coverage) | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 total digitized volumes for the 1780-1810 window; both are detailed above — this is the complete result set for this period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial records, early county records, newspaper archives, military records | In-person / online finding aids at ohiohistory.org |
| County courthouses (Marietta for Washington Co.; Cincinnati for Hamilton Co.) | Deeds, probate, marriages, tax lists from county formation | In-person / mail request |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond VA | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person / written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records, northeastern Ohio genealogy | In-person / https://www.wrhs.org/ |
| Marietta College Special Collections | Ohio Company of Associates records | In-person / written request |
| NARA (Washington, D.C.) | RG 59 Northwest Territory records; Revolutionary War pensions | In-person / Ancestry/Fold3 for digitized |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes and civil suits (Northwest Territory, 1788-1803) — physical at Ohio History Connection and NARA
- Most pre-1800 probate records — physical at county courthouses or Ohio History Connection
- Ohio Company of Associates land purchase records — physical at Marietta College
- Early Methodist circuit rider registers — physical at Ohio Wesleyan University
- Sexton records for pre-1800 burial grounds (survival is extremely limited)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set for the 1787-1803 Northwest Territory/Ohio period was destroyed or lost. Sparse survival of early records is expected for a frontier territory, but absence from online indexes is not evidence of destruction. The Ohio History Connection is the first repository to contact regarding the fate of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Identify the county of jurisdiction first.** A county boundary map for each year 1788-1803 is essential before searching any county-level record. The county that held authority changed repeatedly; searching the wrong county wastes time. The wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory confirms that "boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."
- **Use tax lists as your census substitute.** No reliable 1790 census enumeration exists for Ohio settlers. Annual county tax lists name taxable residents and can track a family year by year through the territorial period.
- **Know which land system your ancestor was in.** Virginia Military District (Scioto to Little Miami rivers): search Virginia State Library for warrants. Connecticut Western Reserve (northeast Ohio): search Western Reserve Historical Society. Everywhere else: search BLM GLO for federal patents.
- **Church records predate all civil registration.** Marriage, baptism, and burial entries in Methodist, Presbyterian, Congregationalist, and Quaker registers are the only vital records for most 1790 Ohio settlers. FamilySearch collection 2246917 is indexed and searchable.
- **Work both before and after statehood as one continuous trail.** A family present in the Northwest Territory in 1790 will appear in Ohio county records after 1803. The break at statehood is administrative, not genealogical — treat territorial and early-statehood records as one continuous research sequence.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio-specific pages (Ohio_Genealogy, Ohio_Vital_Records, Ohio_Land_and_Property) returned only generic content during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for additional research strategies not captured here.

- **Digitized volumes:** 1 browse-only volume of Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records (1788-1799, DGS 005112233, 51 images, 0% indexed, not full-text) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch collection; browse-only for the territorial volume.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (veterans were land-grant recipients in the Virginia Military District and received U.S. bounty land warrants); Northwest Indian War (1785-1795, including the Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrant files at NARA (digitized on Fold3 and Ancestry); state service records at Ohio History Connection for Northwest Indian War militia service
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized pension files

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mound Cemetery (Marietta, 1788, one of the oldest in Ohio); early frontier burial grounds often attached to churches or on family farmsteads with no formal records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage; many early graves were never formally recorded
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive from before 1800 in Ohio

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, 1793) was the first newspaper in Ohio/Northwest Territory; extremely limited survival
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds the earliest Ohio newspaper collections; check their digital resources at ohiomemory.org
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale announcements; obituaries are rarely found this early

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia, Baltimore, and New York were primary eastern entry points; settlers then moved overland or via the Ohio River
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); territorial court naturalizations at the Ohio History Connection
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) for passenger lists; FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants. For families immigrating in this period, check the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property/personal property tax lists; these are the most consistent annual record of residents in this period
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1987542 ("Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850") covers 345,890 records from 1800. A partially-indexed FamilySearch volume of Washington County tax records 1799-1803 exists (DGS 005112240, 73 images, 12% indexed, not full-text).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch (partially indexed for 1799-1803)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records in the 1790-1800 gap and for any census year with missing schedules.

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** The Northwest Territory's legislative and executive records are at NARA (Record Group 59) and the Ohio History Connection. These include territorial land surveys, petition files, and court minutes that name settlers not found in county records.
- **Land company records:** The Ohio Company of Associates (Marietta area) and the John Cleves Symmes Purchase (Miami Valley) left company records naming early purchasers. Ohio Company records are at Marietta College's archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records 1788-1799 (browse-only, 51 images); Washington County Tax Records 1799-1803 (73 images, 12% indexed) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents and surveys | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| NARA | Revolutionary War pensions, bounty land warrants, passenger lists | Free catalog; Fold3/Ancestry for digitized files |
| Fold3 | Military pension files and service records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (partial coverage) | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 total digitized volumes for the 1780-1810 window; both are detailed above — this is the complete result set for this period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial records, early county records, newspaper archives, military records | In-person / online finding aids at ohiohistory.org |
| County courthouses (Marietta for Washington Co.; Cincinnati for Hamilton Co.) | Deeds, probate, marriages, tax lists from county formation | In-person / mail request |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond VA | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person / written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records, northeastern Ohio genealogy | In-person / https://www.wrhs.org/ |
| Marietta College Special Collections | Ohio Company of Associates records | In-person / written request |
| NARA (Washington, D.C.) | RG 59 Northwest Territory records; Revolutionary War pensions | In-person / Ancestry/Fold3 for digitized |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes and civil suits (Northwest Territory, 1788-1803) — physical at Ohio History Connection and NARA
- Most pre-1800 probate records — physical at county courthouses or Ohio History Connection
- Ohio Company of Associates land purchase records — physical at Marietta College
- Early Methodist circuit rider registers — physical at Ohio Wesleyan University
- Sexton records for pre-1800 burial grounds (survival is extremely limited)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set for the 1787-1803 Northwest Territory/Ohio period was destroyed or lost. Sparse survival of early records is expected for a frontier territory, but absence from online indexes is not evidence of destruction. The Ohio History Connection is the first repository to contact regarding the fate of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Identify the county of jurisdiction first.** A county boundary map for each year 1788-1803 is essential before searching any county-level record. The county that held authority changed repeatedly; searching the wrong county wastes time. The wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory confirms that "boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."
- **Use tax lists as your census substitute.** No reliable 1790 census enumeration exists for Ohio settlers. Annual county tax lists name taxable residents and can track a family year by year through the territorial period.
- **Know which land system your ancestor was in.** Virginia Military District (Scioto to Little Miami rivers): search Virginia State Library for warrants. Connecticut Western Reserve (northeast Ohio): search Western Reserve Historical Society. Everywhere else: search BLM GLO for federal patents.
- **Church records predate all civil registration.** Marriage, baptism, and burial entries in Methodist, Presbyterian, Congregationalist, and Quaker registers are the only vital records for most 1790 Ohio settlers. FamilySearch collection 2246917 is indexed and searchable.
- **Work both before and after statehood as one continuous trail.** A family present in the Northwest Territory in 1790 will appear in Ohio county records after 1803. The break at statehood is administrative, not genealogical — treat territorial and early-statehood records as one continuous research sequence.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio-specific pages (Ohio_Genealogy, Ohio_Vital_Records, Ohio_Land_and_Property) returned only generic content during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for additional research strategies not captured here.

The locality guide has been saved to your project as **loc_001**. Here's a summary of what it covers:

---

## California Genealogy — Gold Rush Era (1848–1870)

### Key Starting Points

- **1852 California State Census** — This is your best early population list. The 1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed (several county returns are missing entirely), so the 1852 state census (88% name-indexed on FamilySearch) is the recommended substitute for locating Gold Rush arrivals.

- **1850 Federal Census** — Use with caution; some counties are lost. Still searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry for counties that survived.

- **Great Registers (Voter Registration, from 1866)** — The first systematic statewide name list after the census gap. Even for Gold Rush subjects, these documents where survivors had settled and include birthplace, age, and occupation.

### Mining-Specific Records

- **Mining claim registers** — Digitized on FamilySearch but unindexed; must be browsed image by image by county and date range.
- **County deed and claim records** — Held at county courthouses; document land and claim transactions.

### Immigration & Arrival Records

- **Ship manifests / port arrivals** — NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA) holds San Francisco ship arrival records; some are digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Sacramento port arrival registers** — Digitized on FamilySearch (image browse only).
- **Overland migration records** — Less systematic; check newspapers of the period for party rosters.

### Vital Records

- California did not have mandatory statewide vital registration until **1905**. For the 1850s–1860s, look to:
  - **County recorder** for marriage registers
  - **Church registers** (Catholic missions and Protestant congregations in mining towns)
  - **Cemetery records and funeral home registers**

### Probate & Court Records

- County probate files and court records (estate inventories, guardianship) are held at **county courthouses**. Many from the Gold Rush era document deceased miners whose estates were administered locally.

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 1852 state census, federal censuses, some county records, port arrivals |
| **California State Archives** (Sacramento) | Great Registers, naturalization records, state-level records |
| **NARA Pacific Region** (San Bruno) | Ship manifests, federal court records, military records |
| **County Courthouses** | Probate, deeds, marriage registers, mining claims |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Diaries, letters, newspapers, and manuscript collections from the Gold Rush |
| **California Historical Society** | Photographs, newspapers, local histories |

### Newspapers

Gold Rush–era newspapers (the *Alta California*, *Sacramento Union*, and many short-lived mining-district papers) are a powerful source for arrivals, deaths, and community notices. Check **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) and **California Digital Newspaper Collection** for digitized issues.

---

**Next step:** Narrow to the specific county or mining district where your ancestor worked, then run a county-level locality guide to identify the exact surviving records for that jurisdiction.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California was admitted as the 31st state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely — making it unusual in that it went directly from Mexican governance to U.S. statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the principal commercial and immigration hub.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexican territory (Alta California) until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848); briefly under U.S. military governance 1848–1850.
- **Population during period:** The Gold Rush drew approximately 300,000 people to California from the United States and abroad (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush). The 1850 federal census was the first taken as a state.
- **Economy:** Gold mining (dominant 1848–1855), followed by agriculture, ranching, and commerce. The mining economy produced a transient, predominantly male population from highly diverse origins.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly mixed — Anglo-Americans, Californios (Spanish/Mexican), Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, European (particularly Irish, German, and French), and some African-American. Many groups left distinct record trails.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-statehood via the Mission system), and rapidly growing Protestant congregations (Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopalian) after 1848.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); statehood (1850); massive in-migration 1848–1855; Chinese Exclusion precursors (Foreign Miners' Tax, 1850); completion of transcontinental railroad (1869) accelerated later migration.

## Boundary changes
- California entered as a single state with broadly its modern boundaries in 1850. The number of counties grew rapidly during the 1850s as the legislature carved new counties out of existing ones to serve growing mining districts — records created before a county was formed will be filed under the parent county.
- Before 1850, civil authority rested with Mexican alcaldes (local magistrates) and U.S. military governors. Records from 1846–1850 are sparse and scattered.
- **County formation is critical:** If your ancestor was in a mining district, identify what county that district fell under at the relevant date — it may have changed during the 1850s.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds an indexed collection of California, County Births, 1850-1919 (789,456 records; collection 2017276) and California, County Marriages, 1850-1952 (567,890 records; collection 1452832). These are county-level records.
- **Start date:** The California-specific Vital Records wiki page was not available during this survey (the tool returned only a generic page). The FamilySearch collections indicate county-level birth and marriage recording from 1850. The FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy should be consulted directly for specific registration-start information.
- **Gaps:** Death registration at the county level in the 1850s–1860s was inconsistent; no death collection overlapping this period appeared in FamilySearch's indexed collections for this survey. The transient mining population frequently died far from any registration official.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism registers, cemetery records, newspaper death notices, and probate estate files.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (via the Mission system, pre-1850, and diocesan parishes after 1850), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Episcopalian congregations established in the early 1850s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for Catholic parishes) confirmations.
- **FamilySearch collection:** California, Mission Records, 1769-1850 (98,765 records; collection 1804372) covers the Franciscan mission era and is most relevant to Californio/Native families, not Gold Rush immigrants. For post-1848 Catholic parishes, the Diocese of Monterey (est. 1850) and Archdiocese of San Francisco (est. 1853) archives hold registers; consult them directly.
- **Language:** Mission records and early Catholic parish registers are in Spanish. Protestant records are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (first in California — partially destroyed, some county returns missing per FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records); 1860 and 1870 are complete. Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census.
- **State census:** The 1852 California State Census is the critical substitute for the damaged 1850 federal enumeration. FamilySearch has digitized this; volume 006601001 covers 1850–1852 with 88% name-indexing and full-text searchability — the best single source for locating people in early statehood.
- **Access:** 1852 California State Census — indexed + images on FamilySearch. Federal censuses (1860, 1870) are fully indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, and naturalization petitions.
- **Where held:** County clerk/superior court at the county courthouse. The California State Archives (Sacramento) holds older court records transferred from counties.
- **Naturalization:** Before 1906, any court of record could naturalize — search county, state district, and U.S. District courts separately. Mining-era immigrants who declared intent but died before completing naturalization may appear only in declaration papers, not in a final certificate index.
- **Digitization:** No probate-specific FamilySearch collection appeared for this period. These records are largely physical-only at county courthouses or the California State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a public domain (federal land) state; the rectangular survey system applies to public-land entries. Pre-American land is under the Spanish/Mexican metes-and-bounds ranchos.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexican territory (Alta California) until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848); briefly under U.S. military governance 1848–1850.
- **Population during period:** The Gold Rush drew approximately 300,000 people to California from the United States and abroad (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush). The 1850 federal census was the first taken as a state.
- **Economy:** Gold mining (dominant 1848–1855), followed by agriculture, ranching, and commerce. The mining economy produced a transient, predominantly male population from highly diverse origins.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly mixed — Anglo-Americans, Californios (Spanish/Mexican), Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, European (particularly Irish, German, and French), and some African-American. Many groups left distinct record trails.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-statehood via the Mission system), and rapidly growing Protestant congregations (Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopalian) after 1848.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); statehood (1850); massive in-migration 1848–1855; Chinese Exclusion precursors (Foreign Miners' Tax, 1850); completion of transcontinental railroad (1869) accelerated later migration.

## Boundary changes

The number of counties grew rapidly during the 1850s as the legislature carved new counties out of existing ones to serve growing mining districts — records created before a county was formed will be filed under the parent county.
- Before 1850, civil authority rested with Mexican alcaldes (local magistrates) and U.S. military governors. Records from 1846–1850 are sparse and scattered.

## New York City in the 1700s Colonial Period — Locality Research Guide

New York City was the capital of the British colony of New York Province for most of the 1700s, starting the century with a strong Dutch cultural legacy (the colony had been New Amsterdam until 1664). The most important thing to understand about researching families there in this period is that **there was no civil registration system** — no government office recorded births, marriages, or deaths. Church registers are the only contemporary vital records.

### Church Records (Primary Vital Record Source)

- **Dutch Reformed** registers survive from **1639** and are the oldest continuous series, though they are written in Dutch and must be browsed image by image. FamilySearch holds one digitized volume covering **1700–1776** (211 pages), entirely **unindexed** — you must page through it manually.
- **Anglican (Trinity Church)**, **Presbyterian**, and **Jewish** congregational registers also survive but are not in FamilySearch's digitized set for this period. Access these through:
  - The **church archives** directly
  - The **New-York Historical Society**

### Probate Records

Colonial-era wills went before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (not a county court). The fastest entry point is the **New-York Historical Society's** published indexed series: ***Abstracts of Wills***.

### Land & Other Records

- **Land records** and broader **New York State records** on FamilySearch cover from the 1630s and overlap this period — worth searching.
- **Tax assessment lists** and **colonial militia rolls** can serve as census substitutes, since the first federal census was not until 1790.

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Dutch Reformed registers (digitized, unindexed); New York State land & probate |
| New-York Historical Society | Church registers, *Abstracts of Wills*, tax lists, militia rolls |
| Church archives (Trinity, Dutch Reformed) | Original registers |

### Next Step

Visit the **[FamilySearch Wiki: New York City Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy)** directly for additional record-set detail — the wiki's specific NYC pages could not be fully read during this survey, so further guidance may be available there.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Dutch colony New Amsterdam established 1626; seized by the English 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Administrative center:** Lower Manhattan (New York County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colonial), then New York State (from 1776/1783)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and administrative center throughout the 1700s (Wikipedia)
- **Ethnic composition:** Mixed Dutch colonial legacy, English settlers, enslaved Africans, and various European immigrants; Dutch and English the dominant cultural communities
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, chartered 1697), Presbyterian; smaller communities of Lutherans, Jews, Quakers, and Catholics (Wikipedia, wiki_search)
- **Key historical events:** The city was under British rule for the entire century except for the Revolutionary War period (1776–1783), when it was occupied by British forces; it briefly served as the first capital of the United States in 1789

## Boundary changes
- During the 1700s, New York City was essentially coterminous with the southern tip of Manhattan island, within New York County
- The place_search_all tool returned no historical jurisdictional entries for this place — no boundary-change data was available from the tools
- The transition from British colonial rule to American statehood (1776–1783) changed the governing authority but not the physical boundaries of the city
- Records created under the British colonial government (including those of the Prerogative Court of New York for probate) are held separately from later county-level records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic fallback content — a specific registration start year cannot be cited from this survey. The earliest FamilySearch county marriage collection for New York (id: 1920153) begins in 1847, consistent with no 18th-century civil registration.
- **What exists for this period:** None — church registers are the sole contemporary vital source
- **Where held:** See Church records below
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Dutch Reformed Church registers (from 1639), Trinity Church (Anglican) registers, Presbyterian registers

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers from 1639, oldest continuous series); Anglican/Trinity Church (chartered 1697); Presbyterian; Lutheran; Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation, founded 1654)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations — these are the primary vital records for the entire 1700s
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062) — 2,345,678 records, covering the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume specific to NYC in this period: Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776), image group 007733180, 211 images — **browse-only images (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)**
- **Language warning:** The Dutch Reformed Church registers from the 1700s are written in Dutch — researchers must read or translate Dutch to use them
- **Where held:** Denominational archives (Dutch Reformed records are held by the Reformed Church in America archives and the New-York Historical Society); Trinity Church (Anglican) archives hold their own registers; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Note on parish assignment:** A tool result does not confirm which specific congregation served a given address or ward in the 1700s. Identify the family's denomination first, then locate that denomination's registers.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — only the very end of the target period. No federal census covers 1700–1789.
- **Provincial/colonial enumerations:** New York Colony conducted censuses at various years during the British period; the FamilySearch Wiki Census page for New York returned only generic content and did not list specific years — consult the New York State Archives directly
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of New York City during the colonial period (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Access:** Provincial census records are not indexed on FamilySearch for this place and period; physical or microfilm access through the New York State Archives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianships
- **Colonial probate jurisdiction:** Wills were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York during the colonial period — not the later county-level Surrogate's Court. An index to these wills is published in the *Abstracts of Wills* series by the New-York Historical Society (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780) — 987,654 records, beginning within the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780
- **Mayor's Court:** Court records of the Mayor's Court survive and are a key source for civil disputes, property matters, and other legal transactions (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era grants and conveyances)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants were issued by the Provincial government of New York; the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives hold grant and patent records (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for New York returned only generic content.
- **Types:** Land conveyances, grants, patents, deeds
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654) — 1,567,890 records, beginning within the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan deeds); New York State Archives (colonial land grants); FamilySearch microfilm

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls listing men of military age — useful for identifying residents (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Revolutionary War:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized military records including Revolutionary War pension files
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial militia); NARA (federal/Revolutionary War); Fold3 online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Manhattan, from 1697); Dutch Reformed churchyard; Shearith Israel (Spanish-Portuguese Jewish) cemetery (oldest Jewish cemetery in the U.S., from 1656)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has coverage for some NYC colonial-era burials — check individual cemetery entries
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records held by individual churches and their archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *New York Gazette* was the first newspaper in the colony, operating from 1725 (Wikipedia). Other colonial papers include the *New-York Weekly Journal* and *New-York Mercury*.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — check coverage for specific colonial titles; physical microfilm at the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage and death notices, legal notices, estate sales, runaway servant/slave advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry for NYC
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, naturalization petitions (Mayor's Court and later courts), declarations of intention
- **Colonial-era passenger lists:** The Port of New York has some surviving colonial-era arrival records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov) holds federal-era records from 1820 forward
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including the Mayor's Court and colonial courts
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists by ward survive for some years of the colonial period
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) — 123,456 records — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — covers only 1799–1804, the very end of the target period
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax lists can identify residents in years when no census exists and can document property ownership and economic status
- **Where held:** New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society hold earlier colonial tax records

### Other record types
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Provincial government records at the New York State Archives include correspondence, council minutes, and land grants — a primary source for colonial governance and prominent families (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society:** Holds extensive colonial-era collections including transcriptions and indexes of NYC records (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Abstracts of Wills series (NYHS):** Indexed abstracts of wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York — a critical finding aid for the entire colonial period (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (id: 1469062); New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (id: 2078654); New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (id: 1542780); New York, Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id: 1678432); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776 browse-only volume (DGS 007733180) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War pensions | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including some colonial NYC burials | Free — https://www.findagrave.com |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — check colonial NYC title coverage | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com |
| NARA | Federal records; post-1820 passenger lists; Revolutionary War records | Free catalog; some digitized — https://www.archives.gov |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume specific to New York City for 1700–1800 (the Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776, browse-only). The four state-level FamilySearch collections listed above cover the 1700s period as part of larger date ranges, but are not exclusively NYC-specific.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial census records; colonial land grants; militia records | In-person / online finding aids |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills series; colonial church records; historical newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Colonial-era transcriptions and indexes; NYC vital records transcriptions | In-person; membership database online |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan) | Deed books and conveyances from the colonial period | In-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican (Trinity Church) baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1697 | Contact the archives |
| Reformed Church in America Archives | Dutch Reformed Church registers | Contact the archives or via FamilySearch microfilm |

## Records NOT online
- NYC colonial (non-Dutch-Reformed) church registers for most denominations are not in the digitized FamilySearch volume set for this period
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (New York State Archives) are not digitized on FamilySearch
- Mayor's Court records from the 1700s
- Provincial/colonial census records for New York Colony (pre-1790)
- Most colonial-era ward tax assessment lists (pre-1799)
- Trinity Church and Presbyterian church registers (not found in volume_search results for this period)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific set of NYC colonial records was destroyed or lost. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. To determine the fate of a specific record set, consult the New York State Archives and the New-York Historical Society directly.

## Research tips
- **Church registers are the only vital records for this period.** Identify the family's denomination before searching, because baptism, marriage, and burial records were kept by individual congregations, not a central civil authority. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Dutch Reformed registers require Dutch language skills.** The sole digitized FamilySearch volume for NYC in this period (DGS 007733180, 1700–1776) is in Dutch and is browse-only — plan for either Dutch-language research or find a translated transcription before relying on it.
- **For probate, start with the Abstracts of Wills index before searching the original Prerogative Court files.** The New-York Historical Society published this index covering colonial-era wills, making it a faster entry point than browsing original records. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Tax lists and militia rolls can substitute for absent census records.** No federal census covers 1700–1789; ward tax assessment lists and colonial militia rolls survive for some years and can establish residence and approximate age. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society are the two most important repositories beyond FamilySearch** for this place and period — both hold colonial collections and finding aids not digitized elsewhere. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The FamilySearch Wiki's specific jurisdiction pages for New York (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, Naming Customs) and all four wiki_place_page sections returned only generic fallback content during this survey.** Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly for further research guidance that was not available through the tool.
