Locality guide written as **loc_001** in research.json.

---

New York City was the capital of the British colony of New York Province for most of the 1700s, having started the century as a city with a strong Dutch cultural legacy (the colony had been New Amsterdam until 1664). The most important thing to understand about researching families there in this period is that there was no civil registration system — no government office recorded births, marriages, or deaths. Church registers are the only contemporary vital records. Dutch Reformed congregational registers survive from 1639 and are the oldest continuous series, though they are written in Dutch and must be browsed image by image (FamilySearch holds one digitized volume covering 1700 to 1776, 211 pages, entirely unindexed). Anglican (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, and Jewish congregational registers also survive but are not in FamilySearch's digitized volume set for this period and must be accessed through the church archives or the New-York Historical Society. For probate, colonial-era wills went before the Prerogative Court of New York rather than a county court; the New-York Historical Society published an indexed *Abstracts of Wills* series that is the fastest entry point. Land records, probate records, and church records from the broader New York State series on FamilySearch (covering from the 1630s) overlap this period and are worth searching. Tax assessment lists and colonial militia rolls can stand in for a census, since the first federal census was not until 1790.

The immediate next step is to visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly — the FamilySearch Wiki's specific pages for New York City and New York State returned only generic fallback content during this survey and could not be read, so some guidance that would normally appear in this guide may be available there.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Dutch colony New Amsterdam established 1626; seized by the English 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Administrative center:** Lower Manhattan (New York County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colonial), then New York State (from 1776/1783)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and administrative center throughout the 1700s (Wikipedia)
- **Ethnic composition:** Mixed Dutch colonial legacy, English settlers, enslaved Africans, and various European immigrants; Dutch and English the dominant cultural communities
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, chartered 1697), Presbyterian; smaller communities of Lutherans, Jews, Quakers, and Catholics (Wikipedia, wiki_search)
- **Key historical events:** The city was under British rule for the entire century except for the Revolutionary War period (1776–1783), when it was occupied by British forces; it briefly served as the first capital of the United States in 1789

## Boundary changes
- During the 1700s, New York City was essentially coterminous with the southern tip of Manhattan island, within New York County
- The place_search_all tool returned no historical jurisdictional entries for this place — no boundary-change data was available from the tools
- The transition from British colonial rule to American statehood (1776–1783) changed the governing authority but not the physical boundaries of the city
- Records created under the British colonial government (including those of the Prerogative Court of New York for probate) are held separately from later county-level records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic fallback content — a specific registration start year cannot be cited from this survey. The earliest FamilySearch county marriage collection for New York (id: 1920153) begins in 1847, consistent with no 18th-century civil registration.
- **What exists for this period:** None — church registers are the sole contemporary vital source
- **Where held:** See Church records below
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Dutch Reformed Church registers (from 1639), Trinity Church (Anglican) registers, Presbyterian registers

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers from 1639, oldest continuous series); Anglican/Trinity Church (chartered 1697); Presbyterian; Lutheran; Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation, founded 1654)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations — these are the primary vital records for the entire 1700s
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062) — 2,345,678 records, covering the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume specific to NYC in this period: Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776), image group 007733180, 211 images — **browse-only images (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)**
- **Language warning:** The Dutch Reformed Church registers from the 1700s are written in Dutch — researchers must read or translate Dutch to use them
- **Where held:** Denominational archives (Dutch Reformed records are held by the Reformed Church in America archives and the New-York Historical Society); Trinity Church (Anglican) archives hold their own registers; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Note on parish assignment:** A tool result does not confirm which specific congregation served a given address or ward in the 1700s. Identify the family's denomination first, then locate that denomination's registers.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — only the very end of the target period. No federal census covers 1700–1789.
- **Provincial/colonial enumerations:** New York Colony conducted censuses at various years during the British period; the FamilySearch Wiki Census page for New York returned only generic content and did not list specific years — consult the New York State Archives directly
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of New York City during the colonial period (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Access:** Provincial census records are not indexed on FamilySearch for this place and period; physical or microfilm access through the New York State Archives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianships
- **Colonial probate jurisdiction:** Wills were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York during the colonial period — not the later county-level Surrogate's Court. An index to these wills is published in the *Abstracts of Wills* series by the New-York Historical Society (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780) — 987,654 records, beginning within the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780
- **Mayor's Court:** Court records of the Mayor's Court survive and are a key source for civil disputes, property matters, and other legal transactions (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era grants and conveyances)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants were issued by the Provincial government of New York; the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives hold grant and patent records (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for New York returned only generic content.
- **Types:** Land conveyances, grants, patents, deeds
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654) — 1,567,890 records, beginning within the target period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan deeds); New York State Archives (colonial land grants); FamilySearch microfilm

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls listing men of military age — useful for identifying residents (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Revolutionary War:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized military records including Revolutionary War pension files
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial militia); NARA (federal/Revolutionary War); Fold3 online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Manhattan, from 1697); Dutch Reformed churchyard; Shearith Israel (Spanish-Portuguese Jewish) cemetery (oldest Jewish cemetery in the U.S., from 1656)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has coverage for some NYC colonial-era burials — check individual cemetery entries
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records held by individual churches and their archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *New York Gazette* was the first newspaper in the colony, operating from 1725 (Wikipedia). Other colonial papers include the *New-York Weekly Journal* and *New-York Mercury*.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — check coverage for specific colonial titles; physical microfilm at the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage and death notices, legal notices, estate sales, runaway servant/slave advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry for NYC
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, naturalization petitions (Mayor's Court and later courts), declarations of intention
- **Colonial-era passenger lists:** The Port of New York has some surviving colonial-era arrival records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov) holds federal-era records from 1820 forward
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including the Mayor's Court and colonial courts
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists by ward survive for some years of the colonial period
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) — 123,456 records — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — covers only 1799–1804, the very end of the target period
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax lists can identify residents in years when no census exists and can document property ownership and economic status
- **Where held:** New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society hold earlier colonial tax records

### Other record types
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Provincial government records at the New York State Archives include correspondence, council minutes, and land grants — a primary source for colonial governance and prominent families (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society:** Holds extensive colonial-era collections including transcriptions and indexes of NYC records (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Abstracts of Wills series (NYHS):** Indexed abstracts of wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York — a critical finding aid for the entire colonial period (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (id: 1469062); New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (id: 2078654); New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (id: 1542780); New York, Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id: 1678432); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776 browse-only volume (DGS 007733180) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War pensions | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including some colonial NYC burials | Free — https://www.findagrave.com |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — check colonial NYC title coverage | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com |
| NARA | Federal records; post-1820 passenger lists; Revolutionary War records | Free catalog; some digitized — https://www.archives.gov |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume specific to New York City for 1700–1800 (the Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776, browse-only). The four state-level FamilySearch collections listed above cover the 1700s period as part of larger date ranges, but are not exclusively NYC-specific.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial census records; colonial land grants; militia records | In-person / online finding aids |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills series; colonial church records; historical newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Colonial-era transcriptions and indexes; NYC vital records transcriptions | In-person; membership database online |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan) | Deed books and conveyances from the colonial period | In-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican (Trinity Church) baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1697 | Contact the archives |
| Reformed Church in America Archives | Dutch Reformed Church registers | Contact the archives or via FamilySearch microfilm |

## Records NOT online
- NYC colonial (non-Dutch-Reformed) church registers for most denominations are not in the digitized FamilySearch volume set for this period
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (New York State Archives) are not digitized on FamilySearch
- Mayor's Court records from the 1700s
- Provincial/colonial census records for New York Colony (pre-1790)
- Most colonial-era ward tax assessment lists (pre-1799)
- Trinity Church and Presbyterian church registers (not found in volume_search results for this period)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific set of NYC colonial records was destroyed or lost. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. To determine the fate of a specific record set, consult the New York State Archives and the New-York Historical Society directly.

## Research tips
- **Church registers are the only vital records for this period.** Identify the family's denomination before searching, because baptism, marriage, and burial records were kept by individual congregations, not a central civil authority. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Dutch Reformed registers require Dutch language skills.** The sole digitized FamilySearch volume for NYC in this period (DGS 007733180, 1700–1776) is in Dutch and is browse-only — plan for either Dutch-language research or find a translated transcription before relying on it.
- **For probate, start with the Abstracts of Wills index before searching the original Prerogative Court files.** The New-York Historical Society published this index covering colonial-era wills, making it a faster entry point than browsing original records. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Tax lists and militia rolls can substitute for absent census records.** No federal census covers 1700–1789; ward tax assessment lists and colonial militia rolls survive for some years and can establish residence and approximate age. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society are the two most important repositories beyond FamilySearch** for this place and period — both hold colonial collections and finding aids not digitized elsewhere. — (wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The FamilySearch Wiki's specific jurisdiction pages for New York (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, Naming Customs) and all four wiki_place_page sections returned only generic fallback content during this survey.** Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly for further research guidance that was not available through the tool.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality guide found for tracing Virginia families during the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783):

---

## Virginia Revolutionary War Locality Guide

### Key Sources and Repositories

**1. Military Service Records**
- **FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (collection 1945678) — searchable online, covering state militia and Continental Line units.
- **Federal Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files** at the National Archives (NARA Record Group 15, also on Fold3) — the richest genealogical source, containing sworn depositions that name spouses, children, and specific units served.
- **Virginia Militia Records** — held at the **Library of Virginia** in Richmond.

**2. Tax Records (Critical Substitutes for Missing Census)**
- Virginia's **1782–1785 county personal property and land tax lists** are the essential substitute for the lost 1790 federal census (destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814). These help establish where a family was living during and immediately after the war.

**3. County Court Records**
- Virginia has active county court records dating from the 1630s, making it one of the most record-rich colonies. Deed, will, order, and minute books at local courthouses or the Library of Virginia can document land transactions, estate settlements, and more during the war period.

---

### Important Geographic Caveat
Virginia's 1775–1783 boundaries encompassed present-day **Kentucky and West Virginia**. If your ancestor lived in the western part of the state, records may now be held at courthouses in those states.

---

### Starting Points
- **FamilySearch Research Wiki:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy
- **Library of Virginia** (Richmond) — primary repository for state-level military and tax records

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it operated as an independent commonwealth from 1776 and was formally ratified as a U.S. state in 1788. County-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s.
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1780); Richmond (capital from 1780 onward)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain through 1776; self-governing Commonwealth thereafter
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by FamilySearch tools for this period. The 1790 federal census (the first available) was destroyed and does not survive for Virginia.
- **Economy:** Tobacco, wheat, and iron were dominant; the war disrupted trade and brought widespread military requisitions.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers; significant Scots-Irish and German populations in the western counties; enslaved Africans constituting a large share of the total population.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England / Protestant Episcopal), Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia declared independence in 1776; raised Continental Army regiments and maintained its own militia throughout the war; the Yorktown campaign (1781) ended major combat on Virginia soil.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's boundaries during 1775–1783 encompassed present-day Kentucky and West Virginia.
- Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792.
- Ohio County and Monongalia County (now West Virginia) were active Virginia jurisdictions during this period.
- When researching western Virginia families, confirm which county the ancestor lived in — records may now be at a courthouse in Kentucky or West Virginia, not modern Virginia.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil vital registration existed during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records for confirmed registration start dates by level.
- **What exists:** No state-mandated birth, marriage, or death certificates for this period.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and county court marriage bonds and minister's returns are the primary sources for vital events in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (officially established through the Revolution), Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry books (Anglican), meeting minutes (Quaker).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch indexed collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection 1598230, 1,234,567 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230). Originals are held at individual parishes, the Virginia Historical Society, the Library of Virginia in Richmond, and denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was in 1790, after the war ended. The 1790 Virginia census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; the 1800 census is the earliest surviving federal enumeration for Virginia.
- **State/provincial census:** None taken during 1775–1783.
- **Other enumerations:** Virginia conducted county personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782. These are the most important substitute for the missing 1790 census. FamilySearch volume 005301449 covers state enumerations/tax lists 1782–1799 (87 images; full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image or searched by text string).
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection 1456723, 456,789 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); Library of Virginia holds originals.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, county court minute books.
- **Testate or intestate:** Wills (testate) are in will books at county courthouses; intestate administrations are in the same court records. Both series are in the FamilySearch county court collection.
- **Date range:** County courts were active from the colonial period through the Revolution; records survive unevenly depending on courthouse condition.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection 2134567, 1,789,012 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). FamilySearch volume 005301448 covers Augusta County court order books 1775–1795 (158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed + images). Originals at county courthouses and Library of Virginia.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Virginia Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey. The Library of Virginia and Virginia State Library hold patent and grant records. Post-war bounty land warrant and survey records for veterans are confirmed at the Virginia State Library (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Types:** Deeds, land patents, bounty land warrants (issued from 1779), grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio.
- **Date range:** Patent records date from the 1630s; Revolutionary War bounty warrants were issued 1779 onward.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection 1734285, 2,567,890 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285). FamilySearch volume 005301447 covers Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779–1800 (341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image). Originals at county courthouses and Library of Virginia.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records and muster rolls (NARA Record Group 93); Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia); pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15); Virginia State Navy records.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection 1945678, 345,678 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678). Continental service records at NARA (RG 93); pension files at NARA (RG 15) and on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); Virginia militia records at Library of Virginia, Richmond. The FamilySearch wiki search confirmed the Virginia Military Records page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant application files are especially rich — sworn depositions often name wives, children, ages, units served, and specific engagements.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards and family cemeteries were the norm during this period; formal military cemeteries did not yet exist.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Virginia cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers and vestry burial accounts, where they survive, are held by individual churches or the Library of Virginia.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette was the principal colonial newspaper; multiple competing editions circulated during the Revolution.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Library of Virginia holds microfilm of colonial and Revolutionary-era Virginia papers.
- **Content value:** Notices of military service, Loyalist property seizures, estate administration notices, and lists of deserters or missing soldiers appear in Revolutionary-era papers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Hampton Roads (Norfolk/Portsmouth) was the main Virginia port of entry; many Scots-Irish and German settlers arrived through Pennsylvania.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; few formal naturalization records exist for this period — Parliament-era naturalization and Virginia state legislative acts handled some cases.
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists; Library of Virginia holds relevant state legislative records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax, land tax.
- **Date range:** Systematic county tax lists begin 1782.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection 1456723). Volume 005301449: state enumerations/tax lists 1782–1799 (87 images; full-text searchable, 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image or searched via full-text).
- **Substitute value:** The 1782–1785 tax lists are the standard census substitute for Virginia, replacing the destroyed 1790 census. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Virginia confiscated Loyalist property; claims and forfeiture records are held at the Library of Virginia and Virginia State Archives, naming families on both sides of the conflict.
- **County court minute books:** Record militia musters, road maintenance assignments, and other wartime local government activity — useful for establishing residence and presence when other records are sparse.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (col. 1945678); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (col. 1456723); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (col. 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (col. 1734285); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (col. 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military pension files, Continental Army service records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military and pension records | Free to browse (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 3 digitized volumes match this place and period; all 3 are detailed above (this is the complete result set).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, tax lists, land patents, bounty warrant records, Loyalist forfeiture records, state legislative records | In-person; catalog at lva.virginia.gov |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / College Park) | Continental Army records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person; many items digitized on Fold3 or Ancestry |
| County courthouses (varies by county) | Original deed books, will books, court order books | In-person / mail |
| Virginia Historical Society, Richmond | Church records, family papers, published county histories | In-person; catalog online |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia musters and payrolls (held at Library of Virginia) are not fully digitized.
- The 1790 Virginia federal census does not exist — it was destroyed; no online database can supply it.
- Most county-level church registers survive only on microfilm at the Family History Library or at the Library of Virginia, undigitized and unindexed.
- Loyalist forfeiture and claims records are largely physical-only at the Library of Virginia.
- Volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 341 images) is browse-only with no name index and no full-text search — it must be examined image by image.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. No copies survive. The 1782–1785 county tax lists are the confirmed substitute. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- Some county courthouses suffered losses from fire during and after the Revolutionary period; the Library of Virginia's "Virginia Burned Counties" documentation covers these, but no tool result in this survey names specific counties affected during 1775–1783 — consult the Library of Virginia directly to determine whether the target county's records are intact.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** Federal pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15) are the most genealogically rich Revolutionary War source — sworn depositions typically name wives, children, ages, units, and specific engagements. Accessible via Fold3 and at NARA. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Use the 1782 tax lists as your census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census does not survive, the 1782–1785 county personal property and land tax lists are the standard substitute. Volume 005301449 on FamilySearch covers 1782–1799 and is full-text searchable (not name-indexed — browse or use full-text search). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Check both Continental Army and militia records separately.** Many Virginians served in one but not the other; Continental records are at NARA (RG 93), militia records at Library of Virginia — these are different repositories with different access paths.
- **Track bounty land warrants to Ohio.** Post-war Virginia grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio are a second documentary trail for veterans; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia can confirm service and document migration out of Virginia after the war. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Identify the specific county before searching.** Virginia records were kept at the county level; knowing the county is essential for deeds, wills, and court order books. County boundaries changed frequently during the war period — confirm which county existed at the target date and place.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for the full Virginia research guide.

Here is the locality guide's response:

---

**Locality Guide: New Orleans, Early 1800s — Record Survival & Substitutes**

New Orleans sits at a complicated genealogical crossroads: the city changed sovereigns three times before 1815 (Spanish, French, then American), uses civil law rather than English common law, and lost a large portion of its earliest records to **two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794**. Despite those losses, a surprising amount survives.

**The Most Critical Record Class: Notarial Acts**

Louisiana's civil law system required that contracts, land sales, estate settlements, manumissions, and even informal family arrangements be recorded by a licensed notary. This means someone who left no church register entry may still appear in a notarial document. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds more than 30 million pages of these acts dating to 1734. FamilySearch has only one surviving microfilm volume online (covering 1803–1820, browse-only, in French and English).

**Church Records as a Substitute for Civil Registration**

**St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers**, running from 1731 with gaps, are the primary substitute for civil birth, marriage, and death records throughout the early 1800s. They are partially indexed in the FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925."**

**Key Research Strategies**

- Consult the [Louisiana Genealogy page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) on the FamilySearch Wiki directly, as wiki content for Louisiana-specific pages was limited during this survey.
- Do not assume a record type does not exist online before checking that wiki page.
- Consider probate succession records as another major substitute — Louisiana probate proceedings often documented family members, relationships, and property in great detail even when other records were lost.

**Next Step**

To go further, it would help to narrow down a specific ancestor's name, approximate birth or death year, and which record types (church registers, notarial acts, probate successions) are most likely to produce a match. A targeted research plan can then be built from there.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded 1718 by French colonists. It passed to Spanish control in 1763, briefly returned to France circa 1800, and became part of the United States with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Louisiana was admitted as a state in 1812. (Wikipedia)
- **Parish seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish — Louisiana uses parishes, not counties)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans 1803-1812, then State of Louisiana from 1812
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major Gulf Coast port; cotton, sugar, and international trade. The port generates ship arrival records directly relevant to immigration research.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved people, and — by the 1840s — growing communities of Irish and German immigrants. The multi-ethnic, multi-lingual population means records appear in French, Spanish, and English.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, centered on St. Louis Cathedral from the colonial era). Protestant denominations began arriving in greater numbers after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Battle of New Orleans (1815). Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the period. (Wikipedia; FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

## Boundary changes
- **1763:** French colony ceded to Spain — creates a layer of Spanish colonial notarial and church records
- **ca. 1800-1803:** Briefly returned to France, then purchased by the United States (Louisiana Purchase, 1803)
- **1803-1812:** Records created under the Territory of Orleans; may be filed under 'Orleans Territory'
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted as a state; Orleans Parish continued as the civil jurisdiction for New Orleans
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 predate the target period but their destruction of French colonial records means the effective paper trail for many families begins in the Spanish period (post-1764) or the early American period (post-1803). This is a record-loss gap, not a research failure.

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is noted. Louisiana's civil law system means that notarial records — held at the city/parish level by licensed notaries — perform the function that deeds, wills, and court filings perform in common-law states.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no Louisiana-specific civil registration start year was returned by any tool result. The FamilySearch Louisiana Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) begins in 1819, the earliest indexed civil death data available online per tool results. No corresponding civil birth or marriage index for the pre-1850 period was returned.
- **What exists:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary vital record source for the early 1800s, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Civil registration in this period is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925' (ID 1612905, 987,654 records with images) — free, online. Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records) — index only, no images.
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many pre-1800 records. Parish marriage records before 1837 are not covered by the Parish Marriages collection (1798054) — use church registers or notarial records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant, St. Louis Cathedral). Protestant denominations present post-1803 but not detailed in tool results.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1731 with gaps (wiki_search result).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 ('Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925') is the primary online source. The Archdiocese of New Orleans archives holds the originals.
- **Language:** French and Spanish in the colonial and early American period; English increasingly post-1803. Researchers must be prepared to read the original language.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census available from 1810 for Louisiana (decennial). The 1810 census is the first after the Louisiana Purchase in which New Orleans appears fully as a U.S. jurisdiction.
- **State/provincial census:** No Louisiana-specific state census data was returned by tool results.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (pre-1803) may exist for the earlier period but are not reflected in the tool results for this survey.
- **Access:** The Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection is listed by the external_links_search result (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/, subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** In Louisiana's civil law system, these are 'successions' (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions — distinct from common-law equivalents in other states (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System). Standard probate terminology will not match Louisiana filing headings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 'Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984' (ID 2078341, 456,789 records) covers the full target period.
- **Where held:** Online on FamilySearch (collection 2078341, free). The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records (wiki_search result).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot (arpent) survey system, not the U.S. rectangular survey. This is a distinctive civil-law feature.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Land and Property returned only generic content in this survey — the specific land-grant authority is not confirmed by a returned tool result.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary land record in Louisiana — sales, donations, mortgages, and succession settlements were all notarized. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Date range:** Notarial records from 1734 (with gaps from fire losses). FamilySearch has 1 digitized browse-only volume of surviving microfilm copies covering 1803-1820 (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 167 images, French and English, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical, 30+ million pages). FamilySearch: 1 browse-only microfilm volume.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 and Battle of New Orleans (1815); earlier territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) is listed by the external_links_search result as a military records repository.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/) for federal service and pension records. Louisiana State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The tool results do not name specific New Orleans cemeteries for this period. Catholic above-ground burial (in above-ground vaults) is a distinctive local practice tied to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is listed by the external_links_search result.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers at St. Louis Cathedral and Catholic cemeteries. Cathedral registers survive from 1731 with gaps, per the wiki_search result.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The tool results do not name specific New Orleans newspapers by title or date range for this period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed by the external_links_search result (subscription).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, ship arrivals, legal notices (sheriff's sales, estate notices), and marriage announcements. New Orleans papers in this period ran notices in both French and English.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was itself one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States during the 1800-1850 period. Ship arrival records are directly applicable to New Orleans ancestors.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests), naturalization records. Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record, including Louisiana district courts.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) from external_links_search results.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, poll tax records.

New Orleans in the early 1800s sits at a complicated genealogical crossroads: the city changed sovereigns three times before 1815 (Spanish, French, then American), uses civil law rather than English common law, and lost a large portion of its earliest records to two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794. Despite those losses, a surprising amount survives. The most important record class is the notarial act — Louisiana's legal system required that contracts, land sales, estate settlements, manumissions, and even informal family arrangements be recorded by a licensed notary, meaning someone who left no church register entry may still appear in a notarial document. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Louisiana-specific pages during this survey, so consulting https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly is strongly recommended before assuming a record type does not exist online.

The next step is to build a research plan targeting the specific ancestor or question you have in mind — narrowing to a name, approximate birth or death year, and which record types (church registers, notarial acts, probate successions) are most likely to produce a hit.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded 1718 by French colonists. It passed to Spanish control in 1763, briefly returned to France circa 1800, and became part of the United States with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Louisiana was admitted as a state in 1812. (Wikipedia)
- **Parish seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish — Louisiana uses parishes, not counties)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans 1803-1812, then State of Louisiana from 1812
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major Gulf Coast port; cotton, sugar, and international trade. The port generates ship arrival records directly relevant to immigration research.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved people, and — by the 1840s — growing communities of Irish and German immigrants. The multi-ethnic, multi-lingual population means records appear in French, Spanish, and English.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, centered on St. Louis Cathedral from the colonial era). Protestant denominations began arriving in greater numbers after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Battle of New Orleans (1815). Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the period. (Wikipedia; FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

## Boundary changes
- **1763:** French colony ceded to Spain — creates a layer of Spanish colonial notarial and church records
- **ca. 1800-1803:** Briefly returned to France, then purchased by the United States (Louisiana Purchase, 1803)
- **1803-1812:** Records created under the Territory of Orleans; may be filed under 'Orleans Territory'
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted as a state; Orleans Parish continued as the civil jurisdiction for New Orleans
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 predate the target period but their destruction of French colonial records means the effective paper trail for many families begins in the Spanish period (post-1764) or the early American period (post-1803). This is a record-loss gap, not a research failure.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no Louisiana-specific civil registration start year was returned by any tool result. The FamilySearch Louisiana Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) begins in 1819, the earliest indexed civil death data available online per tool results. No corresponding civil birth or marriage index for the pre-1850 period was returned.
- **What exists:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary vital record source for the early 1800s, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Civil registration in this period is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925' (ID 1612905, 987,654 records with images) — free, online. Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records) — index only, no images.
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many pre-1800 records. Parish marriage records before 1837 are not covered by the Parish Marriages collection (1798054) — use church registers or notarial records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant, St. Louis Cathedral). Protestant denominations present post-1803 but not detailed in tool results.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1731 with gaps (wiki_search result).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 ('Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925') is the primary online source. The Archdiocese of New Orleans archives holds the originals.
- **Language:** French and Spanish in the colonial and early American period; English increasingly post-1803. Researchers must be prepared to read the original language.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census available from 1810 for Louisiana (decennial). The 1810 census is the first after the Louisiana Purchase in which New Orleans appears fully as a U.S. jurisdiction.

Standard probate terminology will not match Louisiana filing headings.

### Cemetery records

### Newspaper records

- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed by the external_links_search result (subscription).

- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

Here is the locality guide for Boston immigration in the 1840s:

---

**Locality Guide: Port of Boston — Immigrant Arrivals, 1840s**

The 1840s were dominated by Irish Famine immigration, and several record types and repositories can help trace ancestors who entered through Boston.

---

### Passenger Lists

The most direct starting point. FamilySearch holds a collection of **Massachusetts Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** (~1.23 million records). A specific digitized volume covers **Port of Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850** (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) — it is full-text searchable but only ~3% name-indexed, so a full-text or browse approach is often needed.

**Important caveat:** 1840s passenger lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and *country* of origin — no hometown and no port of departure. They cannot, on their own, pinpoint where in Ireland, Germany, or elsewhere an ancestor came from.

The **original customs passenger list volumes** are held at the **National Archives at Boston** (physically located in Waltham, MA) under NARA Record Group 36.

---

### Catholic Parish Registers

For the predominantly Irish Catholic immigrants of this era, **parish registers** often supply what civil records lack. Key parishes in the 1840s include the **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's Church**. These records are held by the **Archdiocese of Boston** and contain baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch holds a **Massachusetts Church Records, 1630–1920** collection (~988,000 records).

---

### The Pilot's "Missing Persons" Column

Uniquely valuable for Irish immigrants: *The Pilot* newspaper (Boston) published notices placed by families searching for relatives who had emigrated. This database is accessible via **Newspapers.com** and the **Boston Public Library**, and often names the county of origin in Ireland — filling the gap left by passenger lists.

---

### Massachusetts Town Vital Records

Massachusetts required civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1842. FamilySearch holds **Massachusetts Town and Vital Records, 1620–1890** (~3.46 million records). These can help establish when an immigrant settled in a particular town and provide family details.

---

### Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record, so search both FamilySearch collection **1459213** and **Suffolk County court records**. FamilySearch holds a **Massachusetts Naturalization Records, 1790–1906** collection (~346,000 records).

---

### Probate Records

FamilySearch holds **Massachusetts Probate Records, 1635–1991** (~568,000 records). Probate files can name heirs still living in the country of origin — an important bridge back to the homeland.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, vitals, church, naturalization, probate |
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger list volumes (RG 36) |
| Archdiocese of Boston | Catholic parish registers |
| Boston Public Library | *The Pilot* "Missing Persons" database; city directories |
| Newspapers.com | *The Pilot* and other Boston papers |

---

### Suggested Next Step

If you share the name, estimated arrival year, and country of origin for the specific ancestor you are tracing, a focused research plan can map out which of these collections to search first and in what order.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston settled 1630; incorporated as a city 1822; Suffolk County formed 1643
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place tool for this period. Wikipedia notes that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852).
- **Economy:** Major seaport and commercial hub; one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s
- **Ethnic composition:** Large and rapidly growing Irish immigrant population; also German, British, and other European arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Protestant (Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist); Roman Catholic, centered on the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, serving Irish immigrants
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove tens of thousands of Irish immigrants through the Port of Boston; by 1850 Boston had the highest proportion of Irish-born residents of any major American city

## Boundary changes
- Suffolk County boundaries were stable during the 1840s target period
- No boundary splits affecting record jurisdiction were identified in the tool results

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (FamilySearch collection 2061550, ~3.46 million records) covers the 1840s; this is a **town-level** series recorded at the town of Boston level
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550); originals at Massachusetts Archives, Boston
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not confirm specific registration start dates — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers for immigrant families; see Church Records below

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's — active from the 1840s for Irish immigrants); Protestant denominations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic registers are held by the Archdiocese of Boston archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston); FamilySearch collection 1921657 "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (~988,000 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Language:** English; early Catholic registers may include Latin notations

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 and 1850 censuses cover Boston; the 1840 census names only heads of household with tallied counts, while the 1850 census names every household member and records birthplace — the first census that will directly identify an immigrant
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census collections for the 1840s were returned by the tools
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules begin with 1850 and record deaths in the preceding year
- **Access:** 1850 federal census is fully indexed and name-searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (~568,000 records) covers the 1840s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901); originals at Suffolk County Probate Court, Boston

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal public land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town grants and private conveyances; no federal General Land Office patents for Massachusetts
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds, Boston; not identified as a digitized online collection in the tool results

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) involved Massachusetts volunteers
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Granary Burying Ground, Forest Hills, Holy Cross Catholic cemetery
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Boston-area cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemetery offices

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pilot (Boston Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements — a critical resource for tracing Irish immigrants (Wikipedia: Boston)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Boston Public Library microfilm
- **Content value:** The Pilot's "Missing Persons" column is an important supplement to passenger lists for Irish immigrant families; also covers obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Port of entry:** Port of Boston is the direct port for this research period
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (NARA Record Group 36, 1820–1891); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization in courts of record
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312, ~1.23 million records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 — **indexed + images**
  - "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213, ~346,000 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Digitized volume:** One FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) covers Port of Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850; it is 3% name-indexed but is full-text searchable — not purely browse-only, but not fully name-indexed either
- **Where held:** Originals at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston), 1840s lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. Every person aboard is listed, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family group.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; Boston City Archives
- **Substitute value:** Town and city tax records can locate immigrants between census years

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories were published from the early 19th century and can track an immigrant's residence and occupation between censuses
- **Almshouse / overseers-of-the-poor records:** Document indigent immigrants in the 1840s; held at the Massachusetts Archives and Boston City Archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (1,234,567 records); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (3,456,789); Church Records 1630–1920 (987,654); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (345,678); Probate Records 1635–1991 (567,890) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; overlapping passenger list collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including The Pilot | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — originals for passenger lists (RG 36) and pre-1906 naturalization records | Free (in-person); some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (complete result set) for Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850. collections_search returned 5 collections at Massachusetts scope. Unindexed or microfilm-only holdings at NARA and the Massachusetts Archives may contain additional material not reflected here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists RG 36; pre-1906 naturalization court records | In-person; some records online |
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Town vital records, state court records, land records | In-person / online finding aids |
| Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston) | Probate files 1635–present | In-person / mail |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston) | Deed books, mortgages | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and others) | Contact Archdiocese |
| Boston City Archives | City directories, local government records | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | Historical newspapers, microfilm | In-person / some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Suffolk County deed books (not identified as a digitized collection in tool results)
- Boston almshouse and overseers-of-the-poor records
- The single FamilySearch digitized volume for Port of Boston passenger lists (003345210) is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed — the bulk of records must be located via full-text search rather than a name index
- Catholic parish registers held by the Archdiocese of Boston beyond what FamilySearch collection 1921657 covers

## Known record losses
No tool result specifically identified a destroyed or lost record set for Boston or Suffolk County in the 1840s. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmation of loss. Contact the Massachusetts Archives or the relevant repository before concluding that a specific record type does not survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger lists.** FamilySearch collection 1784312 ("Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891") is the primary indexed entry point. Note that 1840s lists typically contain only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — do not expect a hometown or detailed place of origin (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
- **Search The Pilot's "Missing Persons" column.** This Boston Irish Catholic newspaper published notices by immigrants searching for relatives. It is a major supplement to official records, accessible via Newspapers.com and the Boston Public Library.
- **Catholic church records are essential for Irish immigrant families.** Civil vital registration in the 1840s may be incomplete for recent arrivals; baptismal, marriage, and burial registers from the Archdiocese of Boston archives fill the gap (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston).
- **Search all courts for pre-1906 naturalizations.** A person could naturalize in any court of record before 1906 — federal, state, or local. Use FamilySearch collection 1459213 and also check Suffolk County court minute books.
- **Use the 1850 federal census as the anchor.** It is the first census to name every household member and record birthplace — the earliest census that will name an immigrant directly.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Massachusetts and Boston wiki pages during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records directly for current, specific guidance.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place tool for this period. Wikipedia notes that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852).
- **Economy:** Major seaport and commercial hub; one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s
- **Ethnic composition:** Large and rapidly growing Irish immigrant population; also German, British, and other European arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Protestant (Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist); Roman Catholic, centered on the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, serving Irish immigrants
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove tens of thousands of Irish immigrants through the Port of Boston; by 1850 Boston had the highest proportion of Irish-born residents of any major American city

## Boundary changes
- Suffolk County boundaries were stable during the 1840s target period
- No boundary splits affecting record jurisdiction were identified in the tool results

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (FamilySearch collection 2061550, ~3.46 million records) covers the 1840s; this is a **town-level** series recorded at the town of Boston level
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550); originals at Massachusetts Archives, Boston
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not confirm specific registration start dates — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers for immigrant families; see Church Records below

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's — active from the 1840s for Irish immigrants); Protestant denominations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic registers are held by the Archdiocese of Boston archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston); FamilySearch collection 1921657 "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (~988,000 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Language:** English; early Catholic registers may include Latin notations

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 and 1850 censuses cover Boston; the 1840 census names only heads of household with tallied counts, while the 1850 census names every household member and records birthplace — the first census that will directly identify an immigrant
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census collections for the 1840s were returned by the tools
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules begin with 1850 and record deaths in the preceding year
- **Access:** 1850 federal census is fully indexed and name-searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (~568,000 records) covers the 1840s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901); originals at Suffolk County Probate Court, Boston

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal public land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town grants and private conveyances; no federal General Land Office patents for Massachusetts
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds, Boston; not identified as a digitized online collection in the tool results

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) involved Massachusetts volunteers
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Granary Burying Ground, Forest Hills, Holy Cross Catholic cemetery
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Boston-area cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemetery offices

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pilot (Boston Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements — a critical resource for tracing Irish immigrants (Wikipedia: Boston)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Boston Public Library microfilm
- **Content value:** The Pilot's "Missing Persons" column is an important supplement to passenger lists for Irish immigrant families; also covers obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Port of entry:** Port of Boston is the direct port for this research period
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (NARA Record Group 36, 1820–1891); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization in courts of record
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312, ~1.23 million records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 — **indexed + images**
  - "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213, ~346,000 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Digitized volume:** One FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) covers Port of Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850; it is 3% name-indexed but is full-text searchable — not purely browse-only, but not fully name-indexed either
- **Where held:** Originals at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston), 1840s lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. Every person aboard is listed, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family group.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; Boston City Archives
- **Substitute value:** Town and city tax records can locate immigrants between census years

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories were published from the early 19th century and can track an immigrant's residence and occupation between censuses
- **Almshouse / overseers-of-the-poor records:** Document indigent immigrants in the 1840s; held at the Massachusetts Archives and Boston City Archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (1,234,567 records); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (3,456,789); Church Records 1630–1920 (987,654); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (345,678); Probate Records 1635–1991 (567,890) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; overlapping passenger list collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including The Pilot | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — originals for passenger lists (RG 36) and pre-1906 naturalization records | Free (in-person); some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (complete result set) for Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850. collections_search returned 5 collections at Massachusetts scope. Unindexed or microfilm-only holdings at NARA and the Massachusetts Archives may contain additional material not reflected here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists RG 36; pre-1906 naturalization court records | In-person; some records online |
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Town vital records, state court records, land records | In-person / online finding aids |
| Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston) | Probate files 1635–present | In-person / mail |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston) | Deed books, mortgages | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and others) | Contact Archdiocese |
| Boston City Archives | City directories, local government records | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | Historical newspapers, microfilm | In-person / some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Suffolk County deed books (not identified as a digitized collection in tool results)
- Boston almshouse and overseers-of-the-poor records
- The single FamilySearch digitized volume for Port of Boston passenger lists (003345210) is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed — the bulk of records must be located via full-text search rather than a name index
- Catholic parish registers held by the Archdiocese of Boston beyond what FamilySearch collection 1921657 covers

## Known record losses
No tool result specifically identified a destroyed or lost record set for Boston or Suffolk County in the 1840s. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmation of loss. Contact the Massachusetts Archives or the relevant repository before concluding that a specific record type does not survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger lists.** FamilySearch collection 1784312 ("Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891") is the primary indexed entry point. Note that 1840s lists typically contain only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — do not expect a hometown or detailed place of origin (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
- **Search The Pilot's "Missing Persons" column.** This Boston Irish Catholic newspaper published notices by immigrants searching for relatives. It is a major supplement to official records, accessible via Newspapers.com and the Boston Public Library.
- **Catholic church records are essential for Irish immigrant families.** Civil vital registration in the 1840s may be incomplete for recent arrivals; baptismal, marriage, and burial registers from the Archdiocese of Boston archives fill the gap (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston).
- **Search all courts for pre-1906 naturalizations.** A person could naturalize in any court of record before 1906 — federal, state, or local. Use FamilySearch collection 1459213 and also check Suffolk County court minute books.
- **Use the 1850 federal census as the anchor.** It is the first census to name every household member and record birthplace — the earliest census that will name an immigrant directly.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Massachusetts and Boston wiki pages during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records directly for current, specific guidance.
