---

## Oklahoma / Indian Territory — Native American Records, Mid-1800s

Researching Native American families in mid-1800s Oklahoma means working in **Indian Territory**, a jurisdiction governed by tribal nations and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs — not by U.S. county courts — until Oklahoma statehood in 1907.

### Key Record Types & Collections

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Tribal Enrollment Rolls** | 1851–1959 | FamilySearch: ~567,890 indexed records |
| **Early Land Records** | 1834–1907 | FamilySearch: ~234,567 indexed records |
| **Missionary Church Records** | 1820–1965 | Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian stations; ~123,456 indexed records |
| **Tribal Enrollment Cards** | 1840–1870 | 940 images, 99% name-indexed |

### Most Critical Mid-1800s Sources

- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — key pre-Dawes enrollment source
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — another critical pre-Dawes roll
- **FamilySearch Collection 1987432** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — recommended first online stop

### Repositories for Records Not Yet Online

- **National Archives Southwest Region** — Fort Worth, Texas
  - BIA annuity rolls, tribal court files, federal court records (Western District of Arkansas)
- **Individual Tribal Nation Archives** — each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own holdings

### Critical Caution

All record trails in Indian Territory **split by tribal nation** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, or Seminole records are held separately. Knowing which nation a family belonged to is the **starting point**, not a later refinement.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Identify the tribal nation** your ancestor belonged to.
2. **Search FamilySearch Collection 1987432** (*Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959*) as the first online stop.
3. Follow any finding to earlier pre-Dawes rolls and, if needed, pre-removal records in the southeastern states.
4. Consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at [familysearch.org/wiki](https://familysearch.org/wiki) for tribe-specific place pages.

quirks: Indian Territory was not organized as a U.S. state until 1907 — there were no county courts, no civil vital registration, and no standard U.S. administrative record series during the mid-1800s. Records follow tribal nation authority, not county jurisdiction.
Identify the specific tribal nation (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole, or other) before routing any search — records are segregated by tribe, not by geography.

The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) postdate the mid-1800s target period but capture many individuals born in that era. They are indexed at FamilySearch (collection 1987432) and Ancestry. Earlier pre-Dawes rolls (Old Settler Cherokee Roll 1851, Drennen Roll 1852) are the primary mid-1800s enrollment sources per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls.

Families removed from the southeastern U.S. in the 1830s will have records in their states of origin (Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida) for events before removal. Carry the research back to the removal-era records in those states.

Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons of tribal members) were separately enrolled on the Dawes Rolls as 'Freedmen' rolls for each tribe. Search these in addition to the blood-quantum rolls when researching African-descent family members of tribal households.

The Civil War divided Indian Territory sharply: many tribal members served with the Confederacy; others with the Union. Civil War service records and pension files for Indian Territory soldiers are at NARA and online at Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).

FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Oklahoma returned only generic content during this survey — the Oklahoma_Genealogy, Oklahoma_Vital_Records, and Oklahoma_Native_American_Records pages could not be retrieved via the wiki tool. Consult them directly at familysearch.org/wiki before relying on their absence.

Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) annuity payment rolls function as the mid-1800s equivalent of census or tax records for tribal families; they are held at NARA — particularly the National Archives Southwest Region in Fort Worth, Texas — and are the first stop when tribal census schedules are absent.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma, United States (ca. 1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Designated:** Indian Territory established under the Indian Removal Act of 1830; Five Civilized Tribes relocated via the Trail of Tears (1830s)
- **Tribal capitals:** Tahlequah (Cherokee), Tishomingo (Chickasaw), Doaksville/Tuskahoma (Choctaw), Okmulgee (Creek), Wewoka (Seminole)
- **Parent authority:** Federal United States (Indian Territory); tribal nations governed internal civil affairs as sovereign entities
- **Population during period:** FamilySearch's population tool returned no data for Indian Territory; no standard enumeration existed until the 1890 and 1900 federal censuses included Indian Territory schedules
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, ranching, tribal trade, and later cotton agriculture in the southeastern sections
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes; freedmen (formerly enslaved persons of tribal members); intermarried whites; additional Plains tribes in the western sections
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionary churches established from the 1820s onward, per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act 1830; Trail of Tears (1830s); Civil War in Indian Territory (1861–1865); Dawes Act / allotment (1887+); Curtis Act / Dawes Commission enrollment (1898–1914); Oklahoma statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1830:** Five Civilized Tribes lived in the southeastern U.S. — records for that period are held in their states of origin (Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida).
- **1830–1890:** Indian Territory encompassed most of present-day Oklahoma; tribal nations functioned as sovereign governments within federal authority; no U.S. county administrative structure existed.
- **1890:** Oklahoma Territory organized from the western (Unassigned Lands) portion; Indian Territory remained in the east as a separate jurisdiction.
- **1907:** Both territories merged at Oklahoma statehood; county courts and civil vital registration then established.
- A researcher must identify the specific tribal nation before routing any search — records are segregated by tribe, not by geography or county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey and gave no registration start date; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records directly. Oklahoma statehood (1907) established the civil registration system.
- **What exists for the period:** Tribal enrollment rolls serve as the primary identification documents in place of birth and death certificates. See Tribal Rolls below.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal enrollment rolls, missionary baptism and burial registers (FamilySearch collection 1654321), and BIA annuity payment rolls.

### Tribal enrollment rolls (primary mid-1800s source)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" — collection ID 1987432, 567,890 indexed records with images, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- **Key mid-1800s rolls named in wiki_search:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852); these cover the period before the Dawes Commission enrollment
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Postdate the mid-1800s target window but capture individuals born in that era; indexed at FamilySearch (collection 1987432) and Ancestry; held at NARA Fort Worth per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1987432); the one volume_search result returned for Indian Territory Tribal Enrollment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002298871, 940 images, 1840–1870) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — all maintained missionary stations in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers, membership lists
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" — collection ID 1654321, 123,456 records with 61,728 images, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; covers the full mid-1800s period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed + images); originals in denominational archives and at NARA
- **Language:** English

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" — ID 1987432, 567,890 indexed records with images, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- **Key mid-1800s rolls named in FamilySearch wiki_search results:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852); these cover the period before the Dawes Commission enrollment, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Postdate the mid-1800s but capture individuals born in that era; indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; held at NARA Fort Worth
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1987432); volume 002298871 (Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870, 940 images) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — all maintained missionary stations in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers, membership lists
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" — ID 1654321, 123,456 records with 61,728 images, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Census records
- **Tribal / Indian census schedules:** BIA agents conducted periodic tribal censuses; these are the primary enumeration for the mid-1800s and are included within FamilySearch collection 1987432
- **Federal decennial census:** Indian Territory was not fully enumerated in standard federal schedules until 1900 (Indian Territory schedule) and 1910 (after statehood)
- **BIA annuity payment rolls:** Annual lists of tribal members receiving treaty goods — held at NARA Fort Worth; function as a census substitute for years without an enrollment roll
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is indexed + images at FamilySearch; physical BIA rolls at NARA

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts maintained wills, guardianships, estate inventories, and civil cases for their citizens; the U.S. Court for the Western District of Arkansas (Fort Smith) had jurisdiction over crimes in Indian Territory involving non-citizens
- **Date range:** Tribal court records from the 1840s onward
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth holds federal court records for Indian Territory; tribal nation archives and Oklahoma Historical Society hold tribal court records
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical only or microfilm at NARA and Oklahoma Historical Society; not comprehensively indexed online

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Land in Indian Territory was held communally by tribal nations in the mid-1800s — individual allotment did not begin until the Dawes Act (1887) and Dawes Commission (1898+)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Treaty-based tribal land grants; the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs administered allotment after 1887
- **Types:** Treaty land assignments, tribal land patents, inter-tribal permits; after 1887, individual allotment files
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" — ID 1541872, 234,567 records with 117,283 images, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Indian Territory was heavily contested; Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole soldiers served on both Confederate and Union sides
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls for Indian Home Guard (Union) and Confederate Indian regiments
- **Where held:** NARA; indexed online at Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images at Fold3 and Ancestry for Civil War records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many tribal community and mission cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Mission station burial registers (within collection 1654321); many tribal community graveyards have no formal records
- **Digitization level:** FindAGrave contributor-indexed; mission burial registers indexed + images via collection 1654321

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Cherokee Phoenix (1828–1835, bilingual Cherokee syllabary and English); Cherokee Advocate (Tahlequah)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) listed as external link; also Oklahoma Historical Society digital collections
- **Content value:** Legal notices, removal-era news, community announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant movements:** The Trail of Tears removal (1830s) generated removal rolls documenting families relocated; held at NARA and partially digitized
- **Record types:** Removal/emigration rolls, citizenship applications by intermarried whites and freedmen
- **Content note:** Removal rolls list families including children; examine the full roll for all household members when researching a family
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch collection 1987432 includes citizenship and enrollment records for intermarried persons

### Tax records
- **Types:** BIA annuity payment rolls function as the mid-1800s equivalent of tax lists — annual lists of tribal citizens receiving treaty payments
- **Date range:** From the 1830s treaty periods onward
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth (physical); some digitized within collection 1987432
- **Substitute value:** Essential for years when no tribal census or enrollment roll was conducted

### Other record types
- **BIA agency correspondence and school records:** Annual reports to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs name individual tribal members; Cherokee and Choctaw national school records name students and families; held at NARA, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Freedmen records:** Separate Dawes Roll series for each of the Five Civilized Tribes' freedmen; search these in parallel with the blood-quantum rolls for households of mixed heritage

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (123,456 records); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995 (456,789 records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Dawes Rolls and tribal records; U.S. Federal Census including 1900 Indian Territory schedule | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service and pension records for Indian Territory soldiers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for tribal and mission cemeteries | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for BIA agency records at NARA Fort Worth | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned totalResults: 1 for Indian Territory 1830–1907; that single volume (002298871, Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870, 940 images) was the complete result set. Additional volumes may exist under broader search parameters; the FamilySearch Catalog was not queried in this run and should be checked separately.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth TX | BIA agency records, Dawes Commission files, tribal court records, federal court (Indian Territory) records | In-person; microfilm via interlibrary loan |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Tribal court records, territorial newspapers, state archives post-1907 | In-person; some collections at digitalprairie.org |
| Tribal nation archives (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) | Nation-specific records held by each tribe | Contact individual tribal archives |
| Western History Collections, University of Oklahoma | Manuscript collections, tribal records, Indian Territory documents | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- BIA annuity payment rolls (mid-1800s): held physically at NARA Fort Worth; most not digitized or name-indexed online
- Tribal court records (wills, guardianships, civil cases, 1840s–1890s): at NARA Fort Worth and tribal archives; not comprehensively indexed
- Federal court records (U.S. Court for the Western District of Arkansas, Fort Smith): at NARA Fort Worth, largely physical or microfilm only
- Pre-removal records in southeastern states: held in Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida archives and NARA regional facilities
- Cherokee Phoenix and Cherokee Advocate newspaper archives: physical collections at Oklahoma Historical Society; partial digitization only

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specifically identified a destroyed record set for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s. Many BIA agency records are incomplete due to poor preservation conditions at frontier posts, but no specific loss was stated by any tool result. Consult NARA Fort Worth directly to confirm what survives for a specific BIA agency and date range.

## Research tips
- **Identify the tribe first.** All research paths in Indian Territory branch by tribal nation. The enrollment series, the tribal court holdings, the NARA record group, and the missionary denomination all differ tribe by tribe. Establishing tribal affiliation is the prerequisite step. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Work backwards from the Dawes Rolls.** Even though the Dawes Commission enrollment (1898–1914) postdates the mid-1800s, each card records approximate birth year and blood quantum, pointing directly to the earlier pre-Dawes rolls that cover the mid-1800s. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Search missionary records alongside tribal rolls.** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions (FamilySearch collection 1654321) often contain the only dated vital event for a mid-1800s family and name parents, spouses, and children not separately enrolled. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Check pre-removal records in the southeastern states.** Families removed in the 1830s had records created before removal in Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida. Those archives may hold the only documentation of a family before Indian Territory records begin.
- **Search freedmen rolls separately.** Each tribe's Dawes Roll includes a distinct freedmen series for African American members and descendants of enslaved persons of tribal members.
- **Consult FamilySearch Wiki pages directly.** The wiki_place_page tool returned only generic content for Oklahoma in this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records directly for current collection lists and research strategies.

output.text_response:
Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had **no civil vital registration** — the state didn't require statewide birth, marriage, or death registration until 1906. For Quaker families in that era, **monthly meeting records are the primary vital record substitute**. Here's what to use and where to find it:

---

## Key Record Types

**Monthly Meeting Registers**
Each Quaker monthly meeting kept registers of births, marriages, and deaths, and issued **certificates of removal** when families relocated. These are the single most important source for Quaker genealogy in this era.

**Marriage Records**
Quaker marriages were performed "under the care of the meeting," not by a minister or magistrate, and documented with a marriage certificate signed by dozens of witnesses — a genealogical goldmine for identifying extended kin networks.

---

## Key Repositories

### Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College
The largest collection of Quaker meeting records in the country, including most Philadelphia Yearly Meeting subordinate meetings. Many records must be consulted in person or via microfilm.

### Haverford College — Quaker & Special Collections
Holds additional Philadelphia Yearly Meeting materials and related historical collections.

### FamilySearch
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** (image group 001188322, 145 images) — digitized but browse-only, no name index.
- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** — includes Quaker marriage records; searchable by name.
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — also includes Quaker entries; worth searching first.
- **Pennsylvania County Probate Records** — ~3.2 million browse-only images; useful for establishing family relationships and property.

---

## The Fastest Starting Point

**William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 print volumes) abstracts birth, marriage, and death entries from dozens of Pennsylvania monthly meetings. This is the fastest shortcut for most Pennsylvania Quaker families and is available at major genealogical libraries.

---

## Supporting Records (to fill gaps)

| Record | Where |
|---|---|
| Provincial tax assessments (1750s–1780s) | Pennsylvania State Archives; FamilySearch |
| 1790 federal census | FamilySearch (indexed) |
| County probate files | FamilySearch (browse-only images) |
| Land records / warrantee maps | Pennsylvania State Archives |

---

## Suggested Research Sequence

1. Search **Hinshaw's Encyclopedia** for the ancestor by name.
2. Identify their **monthly meeting** and request the original registers from Swarthmore or Haverford.
3. Search the **FamilySearch marriage compilations** by name.
4. Supplement with **probate, tax, and census records** to establish residence and family structure.
5. Follow **removal certificates** to track migration — Quakers were highly mobile, and certificates document moves between meetings.

---

A practical next step is to identify the county where your ancestor lived, which will point you to the specific monthly meeting responsible for that area and narrow the archive search considerably.

quirks: Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1906 — no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for the 1750-1800 period; Quaker meeting records are the primary vital record substitute (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
Quaker records are organized by Monthly Meeting, not by county or township — identify which meeting served the ancestor's township before searching.
Certificates of removal were issued when a Quaker moved to a different meeting area; search both the sending and receiving meeting's minutes to document a migration.
Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — a single certificate can yield 30-50 witnesses, naming siblings, cousins, and neighbors.

Quakers who violated meeting discipline (serving in the military, marrying outside the meeting) were formally disowned; disownment records in meeting minutes name the individual and often family members.
The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume on FamilySearch (image group 001188322, 145 images, 1750-1800) is browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.
Collections_search returned one entry labeled as a synthetic test fixture (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) — this was excluded from all counts and analysis.

All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and all wiki_read calls for Pennsylvania-specific pages returned only generic fallback content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records directly before finalizing research.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania Colony established 1681 by William Penn; became a Commonwealth in 1776 and a U.S. state in 1787
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early state capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Pennsylvania under the British Crown (before 1776); Commonwealth of Pennsylvania thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool for this period
- **Economy:** Farming, trade, and crafts; Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Welsh, German, Scots-Irish, and other groups; Quakers prominent in southeastern Pennsylvania (Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia Counties)
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) disrupted records and caused Quaker community divisions; many Friends were disowned for military service

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's external boundaries were largely stable during 1750–1800
- County formation continued throughout the period — new counties were regularly carved from existing ones, which directly affects where court, land, and probate records are filed
- Pennsylvania was a British colony until 1776 and joined the United States as a state in 1787

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in Pennsylvania during 1750–1800. The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) states that Quaker records "often substitute for civil registration, which Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide until 1906."
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for this period at any governmental level
- **Gaps:** Complete absence of civil vital records for the entire 1750–1800 period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting registers (births, marriages, deaths) are the primary substitute; see Church Records below

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends) [PRIMARY SOURCE]
- **Record types:** Monthly meeting registers recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disciplinary proceedings including disownments. Marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — making them uniquely valuable as witness lists naming the full community.
- **Geographic focus:** Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia had particularly dense Quaker populations in the colonial and early national periods (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records. Haverford College Quaker and Special Collections (Haverford, PA) holds additional Philadelphia Yearly Meeting materials. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers.
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** One volume — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images). This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be read image-by-image.
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states and is the fastest entry point for most Pennsylvania Quaker research (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Language:** English

### Church records — other denominations
- **Denominations present:** German Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian, Baptist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — organized by congregation, not by county
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings; check both the local congregation and the regional denominational archive
- **Language:** German Reformed and Lutheran records are often in German; a researcher must be able to read the original

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790; it lists heads of household only with tallies by age and sex for other members (not names). FamilySearch has this indexed.
- **Pre-1790:** No federal census; no Pennsylvania state census is known for this period
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania provincial and early state tax assessments (mid-1700s onward) name taxable males and their property and substitute for pre-1790 census data

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** County-level probate records exist from the formation of each county; Philadelphia County records begin in the colonial period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) contains 3,200,560 browse-only images — no records are name-indexed and the collection is not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image-by-image. Physical originals are at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When a Quaker ancestor left a will (testate), search the probate wills series; when no will was filed (intestate), look for letters of administration in the same county records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was a proprietorial colony; land grants originated from the Penn family's Land Office)
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgages; also county tax assessment rolls listing landholders
- **Where held:** The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds colonial-era warrant registers, surveys, and patent books. County recorder of deeds offices hold deed books from county formation. The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey; consult the Pennsylvania State Archives directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Pennsylvania Revolutionary War muster rolls, pension files (NARA), bounty land warrants; the published *Pennsylvania Archives* series (19th century) contains militia and provincial records and is widely available

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had no civil vital registration system at all — the state did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. For Quaker families in that era, the Society of Friends monthly meeting records are the primary vital record substitute: each monthly meeting kept registers of births, marriages, and deaths, and issued certificates of removal when families relocated. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of these records in the country, and Haverford College's Quaker and Special Collections holds additional Philadelphia Yearly Meeting materials; most records must be consulted in person or through microfilm. FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes covering 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images), but it is browse-only with no name index. The fastest shortcut for most Pennsylvania Quaker families is William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 print volumes), which abstracts birth, marriage, and death entries from dozens of Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and is available at major genealogical libraries. Supporting records — county probate files (on FamilySearch as 3.2 million browse-only images), provincial tax assessments, and the 1790 federal census — can fill gaps and establish property and residence. Note that two of the three useful FamilySearch collections for this period (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 and Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900) include Quaker marriage records, making them worth checking by name before going to the physical repositories.

To put this guide to work, a research plan would identify your specific ancestor, map them to their monthly meeting, and sequence a search starting with Hinshaw, then the physical meeting registers at Swarthmore, and then supporting civil and land records.

---

**Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 19th-Century Industrial Research Guide**

Pittsburgh was the heart of American steel production from roughly 1870 to 1900, drawing massive immigrant waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers into the mills. Here's what you need to know:

---

### Key Jurisdictional Points

- **Vital registration gap:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide birth and death registration until **1906**. Allegheny County began county-level registration in 1870, but coverage was inconsistent — especially for immigrant households.
- **City of Allegheny:** Today's North Side was a legally *separate* city from Pittsburgh until 1907. Families living north of the river appear in **Allegheny City** records, not Pittsburgh records, through the entire late-19th-century period.
- **Lost 1890 Census:** The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire, creating a major gap for that decade.

---

### Most Productive Record Types & Repositories

| Record Type | What It Offers | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Federal Census (1870, 1880, 1900)** | Lists occupation, age, birthplace, household members | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **Pittsburgh City Directories (annual)** | Substitute for the lost 1890 census; lists occupation and address | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |
| **Catholic Ethnic Parish Registers** | Baptisms, marriages, burials — often in Polish, Slovak, or Croatian; frequently the *only* vital-event record for immigrants | Individual parishes; Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives |
| **County-Level Vital Records (post-1870)** | Birth/death registration (incomplete) | Allegheny County; PADH microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **Naturalization Records** | Often record exact village of origin in the old country | Allegheny County Courthouse; NARA Philadelphia facility |
| **County Tax Assessment Records** | Good substitute when census or directories fail | Allegheny County |
| **Steel Company Employment Records** | Payroll, hiring records — survive only in fragments | **Senator John Heinz History Center**; **Rivers of Steel Heritage Area** archives (both physical-access only) |

---

### Strategy Tips

1. **Start with census + city directories** to place a person in a neighborhood and mill.
2. **Identify the ethnic parish** for that neighborhood — ethnic Catholic and Orthodox parishes kept the most thorough vital records for immigrant steel workers.
3. **Naturalization records** are a high-priority lead for anyone who arrived as an immigrant; pre-1906 petitions often name the exact European village of origin.
4. **Rivers of Steel** and the **Heinz History Center** are the go-to repositories for anything directly tied to steel company records, union activity, or industrial photographs.
5. For **Allegheny City families**, search Allegheny (not Pittsburgh) in directories, tax records, and court records before 1907.

---

### Next Step

Identifying the specific family, ethnicity, and neighborhood will allow a tighter research plan — particularly for selecting which parish records to target, since ethnic community boundaries in Pittsburgh were very localized.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh chartered as a city in 1816; Allegheny County formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool; the federal census records reflect dramatic growth during the steel boom
- **Economy:** Steel production and associated industries (iron, coke, glass) dominated; Carnegie Steel and other major firms made Pittsburgh the center of American steel manufacturing by the 1880s (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Successive waves of immigrant labor — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers poured into the city and surrounding mill towns (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes by nationality), German Lutheran, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Eastern Orthodox (later Slavic arrivals), and Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 at Carnegie Steel; Great Railroad Strike of 1877 centered in Pittsburgh; rapid industrial expansion 1870–1900; many mill boroughs (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport) operated as separate Allegheny County municipalities

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County was formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties; boundaries were stable during 1870–1900
- The City of Allegheny (today's North Side) remained a legally separate city from Pittsburgh throughout this entire period; it was not merged into Pittsburgh until 1907 — records for families living north of the Allegheny River are under Allegheny City, not Pittsburgh
- Mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne) were separate boroughs within Allegheny County with their own limited local record-keeping

## Available record types

Record-keeping for this period operates at two levels: Allegheny County (marriages, probate, deeds, naturalization) and the city/ward level (some local registration). The federal government held the census and military records.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Allegheny County began county-level birth and death registration in 1870 (per FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records); Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration until 1906
- **What exists:** County birth and death registrations from 1870 (completeness is uncertain, especially for immigrant households); marriage licenses and bonds at the county level from the colonial period onward
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Health Department (birth/death registrations post-1870); Allegheny County courthouse (marriages); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for some pre-1906 materials; FamilySearch collection 1921317 (Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950, 524,189 records) and collection 1571957 (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950, 312,045 records) cover the marriage side of this period
- **Gaps:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates on FamilySearch (collection 2255317, 4.2M records) begin in 1906 and do not cover 1870–1905; the county-level pre-1906 registrations are not widely digitized or name-indexed online
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; census mortality schedules (1870, 1880); city directories

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish), German Lutheran, Episcopal (Trinity Cathedral), Presbyterian, Methodist, Eastern Orthodox
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; ethnic parishes kept separate registers in their native language
- **Where held:** Individual parishes; Diocese of Pittsburgh archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed some Catholic parish registers; the ethnic-language registers require direct parish or diocesan contact
- **Language:** German, Polish, Slovak, and Croatian in ethnic parishes; English in major Protestant denominations

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 are fully available and indexed; all three enumerate occupation and place of birth; 1900 also records year of immigration and years in the US
- **1890:** Nearly entirely destroyed by fire in 1921 — use city directories and tax records as substitutes
- **Mortality schedules:** Exist for 1870 and 1880; they record deaths occurring in the year preceding each census, naming individuals not otherwise captured in civil vital records
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a separate state census
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census records for Allegheny County are indexed and freely accessible on FamilySearch; Ancestry's U.S. Federal Census collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) also carries all three

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories, and petitions — all at the Allegheny County Register of Wills from the county's formation in 1788
- **Date range:** 1788–present; FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) holds 3.2 million images covering this period
- **Access:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch — must be navigated image by image with no name index
- **Research value:** Probate files are a primary source for family relationships when civil vital records are absent; particularly useful for tracing estates of workers killed in mill accidents

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a non-public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) issued warrants and patents; county deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds begin at county formation in 1788; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds original Land Office records (per wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax assessment records at county level; state warrants and patents at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (Pittsburgh); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Note:** Industrial workers were less likely to own land, but annual tax assessment records name all taxable residents and serve as a population proxy

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many fathers of the steel-era generation served; Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Federal Civil War service records and pension files at NARA; pension applications are rich sources for family data; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level enlistment records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC) and NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) for federal records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized pension and service records (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, 1844 — one of the largest 19th-century garden cemeteries in western Pennsylvania); Saint Mary's Cemetery; numerous ethnic-Catholic parish cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Allegheny County coverage; BillionGraves has additional entries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Allegheny Cemetery has published indexes

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (founded 1786 as Pittsburgh Gazette); Pittsburgh Dispatch; Pittsburgh Press (founded 1884); ethnic press in German, Polish, and Slovak
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (strong local collection); Pennsylvania State Library; online via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (newspapers.loc.gov)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and sheriff-sale legal notices, and labor/strike coverage; ethnic-language papers often contain more detailed immigrant community news

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Central and Eastern European immigrants arrived at the Port of New York (Castle Garden, 1855–1890; Ellis Island, 1892–1954); Irish and German immigrants also arrived at Baltimore and Philadelphia
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA; naturalization records (declarations of intention and petitions) at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas and at the federal district court (NARA Philadelphia)
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch volume 008120443 (Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, bilingual English/German); also search Ancestry's U.S. Naturalization Records collection
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person in the party, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. The 1900–1906 manifests added fields for last residence abroad and US contact person, critical for tracing chain migration into Pittsburgh mill communities.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki states Catholic parishes were essential for immigrant family data — "their registers are often the best source for family data" for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and real estate tax assessment records, collected annually at the township/ward level
- **Date range:** Allegheny County assessment records survive from the late 1700s through the period
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; Pennsylvania State Archives holds some duplicate assessment records
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment records for 1890 can partially substitute for the destroyed 1890 census — presence in that year's list confirms the family's residence in the county

### Occupational and industrial records (steel-era specific)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary; some Carnegie Steel and related company records survive at the Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives — these are physical-only and not digitized (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union records:** Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers records survive variably; union membership lists are the most useful genealogical source when they exist
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward (per same FamilySearch Wiki source); directories for 1870–1900 list every head of household with occupation and address — one of the most reliable annual population proxies for this period
- **State factory inspection reports:** Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports from 1872 onward, naming workplaces; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and major research libraries
- **Social surveys:** The Pittsburgh Survey (1907–1908, Russell Sage Foundation) documented living and working conditions in the steel communities; slightly post-period but names neighborhoods and provides context for interpreting earlier records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317, 524K records); Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957, 312K records); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909, 199K records); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 351 images, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900; naturalization records; city directories | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and Pittsburgh Press runs | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Allegheny County | Free |
| NARA | Federal records — passenger lists, federal court naturalizations (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania in the 1870–1900 window; the tool confirmed this is the complete result set (complete: true). Significant digitized collections for Pittsburgh/Allegheny County also exist through Ancestry and are not fully represented in these 3 FamilySearch volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Register of Wills | Probate records 1788–present | In-person / mail |
| Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books 1788–present | In-person |
| Allegheny County Health Department | Birth/death registrations 1870–present | Mail / application |
| Allegheny County courthouse | Marriage licenses colonial–present; pre-1906 naturalization records | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Land Office records, state military records, factory inspection reports | In-person / online request |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records (fragmentary), city directories, local history | In-person |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area | Steel industry company archives | In-person / by appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories 1810s–present; newspapers; local history | In-person |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh archives | Catholic parish registers | By request |

## Records NOT online
- County-level birth and death registrations for 1870–1905 (the Allegheny County pre-statewide series) are not broadly digitized or name-indexed online
- Steel company employment records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives are physical-only
- Union membership records, where they survive, are held by individual union archives and are not online
- Pennsylvania factory inspection reports are at the Pennsylvania State Archives, physical only
- Many ethnic Catholic parish registers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) have not been digitized and must be accessed through individual parishes or the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives
- Annual tax assessment records for Allegheny County are at the county level and are largely not digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was nearly entirely destroyed by fire in 1921 — this is a national loss, not specific to Allegheny County. No tool result identified additional losses specific to Allegheny County records in this period. City directories, tax assessments, and the 1880/1900 census are the primary substitutes for the missing 1890 year.

## Research tips
- **Start with the federal census.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules for Allegheny County all record occupation and place of birth; 1900 also gives year of immigration and years in the US — these are the backbone of any steel-worker family reconstruction
- **City directories are annual proxies.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's collection (described at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) covers Pittsburgh from the 1810s forward and lists occupations and addresses year by year; use them to track a family between censuses and to identify which mill employed a worker
- **Naturalization records name the home village.** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions filed in Allegheny County courts often recorded the immigrant's exact town of origin — this unlocks the foreign church and civil records. Search both the county court records and NARA's Philadelphia regional holdings (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)
- **Ethnic parishes are the best vital-record substitute before 1906.** Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records); for 1870–1905, Catholic baptismal and burial registers are often the only documentation of a birth or death — identify the parish by neighborhood and nationality, then contact the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives
- **Allegheny City is not Pittsburgh before 1907.** The independent City of Allegheny (today's North Side) had separate record-keeping; families north of the Allegheny River appear in Allegheny City records until the 1907 annexation
- **Mortality schedules fill gaps for pre-1906 deaths.** The 1870 and 1880 census mortality schedules list deaths in the preceding year by name, age, and cause — an important substitute for pre-1906 vital records

- **Research value:** Probate files are a primary source for family relationships when civil vital records are absent; particularly useful for tracing estates of workers killed in mill accidents

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a non-public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) issued warrants and patents; county deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds begin at county formation in 1788; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds original Land Office records (per wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax assessment records at county level; state warrants and patents at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (Pittsburgh); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Note:** Industrial workers were less likely to own land, but annual tax assessment records name all taxable residents and serve as a population proxy

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many fathers of the steel-era generation served; Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Federal Civil War service records and pension files at NARA; pension applications are rich sources for family data; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level enlistment records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC) and NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) for federal records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized pension and service records (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, 1844 — one of the largest 19th-century garden cemeteries in western Pennsylvania); Saint Mary's Cemetery; numerous ethnic-Catholic parish cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Allegheny County coverage; BillionGraves has additional entries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Allegheny Cemetery has published indexes

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (founded 1786 as Pittsburgh Gazette); Pittsburgh Dispatch; Pittsburgh Press (founded 1884); ethnic press in German, Polish, and Slovak
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (strong local collection); Pennsylvania State Library; online via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (newspapers.loc.gov)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and sheriff-sale legal notices, and labor/strike coverage; ethnic-language papers often contain more detailed immigrant community news

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Central and Eastern European immigrants arrived at the Port of New York (Castle Garden, 1855–1890; Ellis Island, 1892–1954); Irish and German immigrants also arrived at Baltimore and Philadelphia
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA; naturalization records (declarations of intention and petitions) at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas and at the federal district court (NARA Philadelphia)
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch volume 008120443 (Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, bilingual English/German); also search Ancestry's U.S. Naturalization Records collection
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person in the party, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. The 1900–1906 manifests added fields for last residence abroad and US contact person, critical for tracing chain migration into Pittsburgh mill communities.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki states Catholic parishes were essential for immigrant family data — "their registers are often the best source for family data" for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and real estate tax assessment records, collected annually at the township/ward level
- **Date range:** Allegheny County assessment records survive from the late 1700s through the period
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; Pennsylvania State Archives holds some duplicate assessment records
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment records for 1890 can partially substitute for the destroyed 1890 census — presence in that year's list confirms the family's residence in the county

### Occupational and industrial records (steel-era specific)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary; some Carnegie Steel and related company records survive at the Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives — these are physical-only and not digitized (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union records:** Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers records survive variably; union membership lists are the most useful genealogical source when they exist
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward (per same FamilySearch Wiki source); directories for 1870–1900 list every head of household with occupation and address — one of the most reliable annual population proxies for this period
- **State factory inspection reports:** Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports from 1872 onward, naming workplaces; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and major research libraries
- **Social surveys:** The Pittsburgh Survey (1907–1908, Russell Sage Foundation) documented living and working conditions in the steel communities; slightly post-period but names neighborhoods and provides context for interpreting earlier records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317, 524K records); Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957, 312K records); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909, 199K records); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 351 images, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900; naturalization records; city directories | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and Pittsburgh Press runs | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Allegheny County | Free |
| NARA | Federal records — passenger lists, federal court naturalizations (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania in the 1870–1900 window; the tool confirmed this is the complete result set (complete: true). Significant digitized collections for Pittsburgh/Allegheny County also exist through Ancestry and are not fully represented in these 3 FamilySearch volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Register of Wills | Probate records 1788–present | In-person / mail |
| Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books 1788–present | In-person |
| Allegheny County Health Department | Birth/death registrations 1870–present | Mail / application |
| Allegheny County courthouse | Marriage licenses colonial–present; pre-1906 naturalization records | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Land Office records, state military records, factory inspection reports | In-person / online request |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records (fragmentary), city directories, local history | In-person |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area | Steel industry company archives | In-person / by appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories 1810s–present; newspapers; local history | In-person |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh archives | Catholic parish registers | By request |

## Records NOT online
- County-level birth and death registrations for 1870–1905 (the Allegheny County pre-statewide series) are not broadly digitized or name-indexed online
- Steel company employment records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives are physical-only
- Union membership records, where they survive, are held by individual union archives and are not online
- Pennsylvania factory inspection reports are at the Pennsylvania State Archives, physical only
- Many ethnic Catholic parish registers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) have not been digitized and must be accessed through individual parishes or the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives
- Annual tax assessment records for Allegheny County are at the county level and are largely not digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was nearly entirely destroyed by fire in 1921 — this is a national loss, not specific to Allegheny County. No tool result identified additional losses specific to Allegheny County records in this period. City directories, tax assessments, and the 1880/1900 census are the primary substitutes for the missing 1890 year.

## Research tips
- **Start with the federal census.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules for Allegheny County all record occupation and place of birth; 1900 also gives year of immigration and years in the US — these are the backbone of any steel-worker family reconstruction
- **City directories are annual proxies.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's collection (described at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) covers Pittsburgh from the 1810s forward and lists occupations and addresses year by year; use them to track a family between censuses and to identify which mill employed a worker
- **Naturalization records name the home village.** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions filed in Allegheny County courts often recorded the immigrant's exact town of origin — this unlocks the foreign church and civil records. Search both the county court records and NARA's Philadelphia regional holdings (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)
- **Ethnic parishes are the best vital-record substitute before 1906.** Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records); for 1870–1905, Catholic baptismal and burial registers are often the only documentation of a birth or death — identify the parish by neighborhood and nationality, then contact the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives
- **Allegheny City is not Pittsburgh before 1907.** The independent City of Allegheny (today's North Side) had separate record-keeping; families north of the Allegheny River appear in Allegheny City records until the 1907 annexation
- **Mortality schedules fill gaps for pre-1906 deaths.** The 1870 and 1880 census mortality schedules list deaths in the preceding year by name, age, and cause — an important substitute for pre-1906 vital records

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Philadelphia in 1793 was a city of roughly 50,000 people, about one-tenth of whom died in the yellow fever epidemic that ran from August through November of that year. Because Pennsylvania had no civil vital registration at the time, church burial registers are the only structured death records for epidemic victims. The most immediately useful sources are the burial registers of Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church), Mathew Carey's published 1793 account naming many of the dead, and the manuscript minutes of the citizens' relief Committee and Bush Hill hospital records, all held physically at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. FamilySearch has very sparse digitized coverage for Philadelphia in this period: one browse-only volume of Quaker Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800) and several Pennsylvania-wide probate and marriage collections whose pre-1800 images must be browsed page by page with no name index. The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses, available indexed online, are the best population anchors before and after the epidemic. Philadelphia Orphans' Court records at the Philadelphia City Archives are a particularly underused source for epidemic research, since so many sudden deaths left minor children requiring court-appointed guardians.

The next step would be to identify which specific family or individual you are tracing so that a targeted research plan can direct which of these repositories and record types to work first.

Probate filings spike in 1793-1795 following epidemic deaths — Philadelphia County probate records (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 on FamilySearch) are browse-only images with no name index and must be searched page by page.
The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Quakers), 1750–1800, are digitized on FamilySearch (image group 001188322, 145 images) but are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.

Bush Hill hospital records and the minutes of the Committee appointed by citizens are manuscript sources held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania — not digitized on FamilySearch.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1785–1805, Yellow Fever Epidemic Focus)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; co-extensive with the city after the Act of Consolidation of 1854 (outside our period)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 42,000–55,000 in the 1790s (the 1793 epidemic killed roughly 5,000 people — about one-tenth of residents, per the Wikipedia article on the Yellow fever epidemic of 1793)
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; shipping, trade, crafts, and early manufacturing dominate; the city was the national capital through 1800
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English and German Protestant, with Irish, African American (both free and enslaved), and smaller French refugee communities; French West Indian refugees arrived in 1793 and contributed to epidemic spread
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Quaker (Society of Friends), German Reformed, German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November 1793); approximately 5,000 dead, thousands more fled; the federal government evacuated; epidemic recurred in smaller form in later years of the 1790s

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County boundaries were stable throughout the target period (1785–1805)
- The city of Philadelphia and surrounding townships (Northern Liberties, Southwark, Moyamensing, etc.) were separate municipalities within the county; records may be filed at the township or county level depending on the record type
- The Act of Consolidation (1854) merged city and county, but this is outside the research period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" begins in 1906, indicating statewide registration did not commence until the early twentieth century. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and could not be consulted for specific registration dates.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates existed. Church registers are the only structured vital records.
- **Pre-registration substitutes:** Church burial registers, Mathew Carey's published list of the dead, newspaper death notices, and probate filings
- **Gaps:** The crisis conditions of August–November 1793 led to hasty or incomplete burial record-keeping at many churches

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Episcopal/Anglican (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes', established 1677, the oldest surviving church in Pennsylvania), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), German Reformed, German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Quaker meeting minutes record births, marriages, and deaths
- **The 1793 epidemic and church records:** The FamilySearch Wiki genealogy search (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) identifies burial records from Christ Church and Gloria Dei as key sources for epidemic victims. Many churches recorded a surge of burials in late summer and autumn of 1793.
- **Where held:** Original registers at individual church archives and diocesan repositories; many have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania; FamilySearch has microfilmed some Philadelphia church records
- **Digitization level:** Varies by congregation; the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Quakers), 1750–1800, are on FamilySearch (image group 001188322, 145 images) but are browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable
- **Language:** English for most; Latin for some Catholic registers; Swedish and Latin for early Gloria Dei records

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793)
- **Mathew Carey's account:** "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) names many of the dead and survivors; it is a published primary source widely held in research libraries and available in digitized form through major library databases
- **Committee minutes:** The minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by citizens to manage the epidemic response name individuals who received relief and those who died; held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (manuscript, not digitized on FamilySearch)
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the city's fever hospital; held at the Philadelphia City Archives (manuscript, physical access required)
- **Source citation:** FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (pre-epidemic) and the 1800 federal census (post-epidemic) are the primary population snapshots. The 1790 census shows household composition before 1793; the 1800 census reveals which households survived, contracted, or reconstituted. Both are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **State/territorial census:** Pennsylvania conducted no state census in this period
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia tax lists (often annual) function as intercensal substitutes and can document year-by-year changes in household composition or property
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed online; Philadelphia tax lists are largely physical records at the Philadelphia City Archives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), inventories, guardianships
- **Epidemic connection:** Probate filings spike sharply in 1793–1795 as estates of epidemic victims were settled; for anyone believed to have died in or just after the epidemic, search Philadelphia County probate for this window
- **Testate or intestate:** Many epidemic deaths were sudden, leaving estates intestate (no will) — search letters of administration as well as wills in the 1793–1795 period
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records survive from the colonial period through the present
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) contains 3,200,560 browse-only images — no name index and not full-text searchable; must be browsed page by page
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Register of Wills; FamilySearch has digitized images (browse-only); Philadelphia City Archives holds additional probate-related manuscripts

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was a proprietary colony; no rectangular-survey system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original land warrant and patent records from the proprietary and Commonwealth periods
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (a Philadelphia-specific instrument common in this era), tax records
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds for deeds and mortgages; Pennsylvania State Archives for pre-statehood and early Commonwealth grants; Philadelphia City Archives for tax records
- **Digitization level:** Philadelphia deed books for this period are largely physical; some FamilySearch microfilm holdings exist but extent was not confirmed in this survey's volume search

### Military records

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Philadelphia in 1793 was a city of roughly 50,000 people, about one-tenth of whom died in the yellow fever epidemic that ran from August through November of that year. Because Pennsylvania had no civil vital registration at the time, church burial registers are the only structured death records for epidemic victims. The most immediately useful sources are the burial registers of Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church), Mathew Carey's published 1793 account naming many of the dead, and the manuscript minutes of the citizens' relief Committee and Bush Hill hospital records, all held physically at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. FamilySearch has very sparse digitized coverage for Philadelphia in this period: one browse-only volume of Quaker Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750-1800) and several Pennsylvania-wide probate and marriage collections whose pre-1800 images must be browsed page by page with no name index. The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses, available indexed online, are the best population anchors before and after the epidemic. Philadelphia Orphans' Court records at the Philadelphia City Archives are a particularly underused source for epidemic research, since so many sudden deaths left minor children requiring court-appointed guardians.

The next step would be to identify which specific family or individual you are tracing so that a targeted research plan can direct which of these repositories and record types to work first.

- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; shipping, trade, crafts, and early manufacturing dominate; the city was the national capital through 1800
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English and German Protestant, with Irish, African American (both free and enslaved), and smaller French refugee communities; French West Indian refugees arrived in 1793 and contributed to epidemic spread
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Quaker (Society of Friends), German Reformed, German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November 1793); approximately 5,000 dead, thousands more fled; the federal government evacuated; epidemic recurred in smaller form in later years of the 1790s

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County boundaries were stable throughout the target period (1785–1805)
- The city of Philadelphia and surrounding townships (Northern Liberties, Southwark, Moyamensing, etc.) were separate municipalities within the county; records may be filed at the township or county level depending on the record type
- The Act of Consolidation (1854) merged city and county, but this is outside the research period

The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" begins in 1906, indicating statewide registration did not commence until the early twentieth century. - **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates existed. Church registers are the only structured vital records.
- **Pre-registration substitutes:** Church burial registers, Mathew Carey's published list of the dead, newspaper death notices, and probate filings
